options: Malware that encrypts the victim’s files and demands payment (ransom) to restore access
A proprietary Cisco protocol used only to synchronize the internal NTP clocks
An extended ACL that allows only HTTPS traffic and blocks every other flow on the LAN
A type of multimode fiber-optic cable used only for short links inside a building
en.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and demands ransom. Related malware types include viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, and rootkits. Mitigations: offline backups, patching, MFA, email filtering, and least privilege.

en.question: What is Zero Trust, in terms of network security principles?
options: Automatically trust any device that sits inside the corporate LAN, without checking its identity again
Turn off all perimeter firewalls because the provider cloud is treated as secure by default, with no inspection
Never trust by default: continuously verify identity, context, and posture before granting least-privilege access
Use only shared passwords on the LAN access switches, with no individual authentication for each user or port
en.explanation: Zero Trust assumes the internal network is not an automatic trust zone. It requires strong authentication, contextual authorization, microsegmentation, and continuous verification (never trust, always verify).

en.question: In the Cisco security ecosystem, what is the typical role of Cisco ISE (Identity Services Engine) versus a unified XDR/visibility platform such as SecureX (or successors)?
options: ISE completely replaces BGP routing on the Internet, advertising public prefixes and external routes in place of the organization's own border routers and upstream ISPs
ISE focuses on identity, access control (802.1X, guest, posture) and policy; SecureX-class platforms aggregate telemetry and orchestrate response across products
SecureX is only a serial console cable plugged into the router console port; ISE is only a decorative wallpaper theme on the device startup screen
Both exist solely to configure access VLANs on unmanaged switches, with no role in identity, posture assessment, or response orchestration
en.explanation: Cisco ISE is the AAA/NAC policy engine (802.1X, profiling, posture, guest). SecureX-class platforms integrate alerts and workflows across firewall, endpoint, email, and more. They complement each other in Cisco security architecture.

en.question: What is the fundamental difference between hashing and symmetric encryption?
options: Hashing and encryption are always the same AES-256 algorithm, with the same secret key and the same reversible result in both cases
Encryption only works on text written in Portuguese; hashing only yields a valid result when the original text is in English
Hashing always increases the size of the original data in each block; symmetric encryption always shrinks the message to exactly 128 bits
Hashing is typically one-way (integrity/verification); symmetric encryption is reversible with the shared key (confidentiality)
en.explanation: Hashes (SHA-256, etc.) are not reversed to recover the original — they support integrity and verification. Symmetric encryption (AES) encrypts and decrypts with the same key. Asymmetric crypto uses public/private key pairs.

en.question: Why does multi-factor authentication (MFA) significantly reduce account-compromise risk?
options: Because it removes entirely the need for operating-system security patches, leaving software flaws uncorrected on every host
Because it makes Wi-Fi automatically WPA3 with no configuration at all, even on old access points that only support WPA2
Because it replaces perimeter firewalls in every scenario, so filtering rules are no longer required at the network edge
Because it requires more than just a password (e.g., OTP app, token, biometrics), making stolen credentials harder to abuse
en.explanation: MFA combines factors (knowledge, possession, inherence). Even with a leaked password, the attacker still needs the second factor. It is essential in Zero Trust and for privileged Cisco access — and it does not replace patching or firewalls.

en.question: What is defense in depth in a network environment?
options: Using one complex password for every network device, shared across the routers, the switches, and the firewalls on the local network
Relying only on endpoint antivirus and removing all network segmentation, so the internal LAN remains a single trust zone
Applying multiple layers of controls (perimeter, network, identity, endpoint, data) so one failure does not compromise everything
Disabling security logs to improve device performance, without recording failed access attempts or any configuration changes
en.explanation: Defense in depth stacks complementary controls: firewalls, segmentation, AAA/MFA, EDR, encryption, and monitoring. It reduces the impact of any single failure.

en.question: What is the main cybersecurity benefit of network segmentation (e.g., VLANs, firewalls between zones)?
options: Enlarging each VLAN broadcast domain so malware spreads faster among hosts in the same zone and across neighboring zones
Removing the need to update firmware on switches, firewalls, and routers by treating segmentation as a substitute for security patches
Letting guests share the same management VLAN as the routers and firewalls, with direct access to the administrative IP addresses
Limiting lateral movement: a compromise in one zone does not automatically reach critical servers in another
en.explanation: Segmentation (and microsegmentation) restricts east-west traffic. It isolates IoT/guest from management and data centers, aligned with Zero Trust and least privilege.

en.question: What is the primary purpose of a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform?
options: Replacing every endpoint antivirus agent with a single packet broker on the core switch, which then inspects malicious files on the host itself
Issuing public TLS certificates for internal servers without a private CA, signing internal names as if it were a public certificate authority
Collecting and correlating logs/events from many sources, detecting suspicious patterns, and supporting alerting and investigation
Guaranteeing zero false positives by blocking all outbound DNS queries so that no external name can be resolved by clients
en.explanation: A SIEM aggregates logs and security events (firewalls, endpoints, identity, cloud, etc.), normalizes and correlates them, and helps analysts detect, alert on, and investigate incidents. It does not replace AV with a packet broker, does not act as a public CA for TLS, and cannot promise zero false positives by blindly blocking DNS.

en.question: In cybersecurity, what is the MITRE ATT&CK framework mainly used for?
options: A vendor-specific CLI syntax guide for configuring ASA access lists, including access-list and access-group, ACE order, and the implicit deny at the end of every extended ACL
A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques (and related procedures) used to map detections, plan defenses, and communicate about threats in a common language
A mandatory encryption algorithm that replaces AES in all TLS 1.3 handshakes, forcing one symmetric cipher in every ClientHello and refusing every other negotiated cipher suite
A physical rack layout standard for data-center cabling density that fixes rack-unit height, vertical cable managers, and the spacing of copper and fiber patch panels
en.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK catalogs real-world adversary tactics (the “why”) and techniques (the “how”), often with procedure examples. Defenders use it to gap-analyze coverage, write detections, and discuss incidents consistently. It is not ASA CLI documentation, not a cipher that replaces AES, and not a cabling standard.

en.question: What does a Web Application Firewall (WAF) primarily protect against?
options: Application-layer attacks against HTTP/HTTPS apps (for example SQLi, XSS, and abuse of vulnerable URLs or APIs), by inspecting and filtering web requests
Layer 1 cable cuts between the access switch and the end user PC, when the copper pair or fiber loses continuity and the Ethernet link loses signal at the wall jack
Exhaustion of OSPF LSDB memory on core routers caused by too many Type 5 LSAs for external routes redistributed from other routing protocols
Battery failure in a UPS that powers the wireless controllers, leaving the access points without power during an electrical outage in the rack
en.explanation: A WAF sits in front of web applications and inspects HTTP/S traffic to block or challenge common app-layer attacks such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and known bad request patterns. It does not fix physical cable cuts, OSPF LSDB sizing, or UPS batteries.

en.question: What is the primary purpose of DNSSEC?
options: Encrypting each DNS query so the recursive resolver never sees the name being looked up (that is DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS, not DNSSEC), hiding the QNAME on the wire
Replacing SPF so mail servers no longer need to check which hosts may send for a domain, ignoring the TXT record and accepting any sending MTA
Digitally signing DNS data so validating resolvers can detect forged or tampered answers (authenticity and integrity), without hiding the query itself
Automatically blocking every malware download on the endpoint by deleting the fetched file before any local process is able to execute it
en.explanation: DNSSEC adds digital signatures (RRSIG and DNSKEY records, chained with DS records in the parent) so a validating resolver can confirm that the data came from the authoritative zone and was not modified. Query confidentiality comes from DoT or DoH, not from DNSSEC. It does not replace email authentication or endpoint protection.

en.question: Working together, what do SPF, DKIM, and DMARC do for email security?
options: They encrypt the message body end to end so only the recipient can read it (that is S/MIME or PGP), ciphering the content with the recipient public key before submission
SPF lists which servers may send for a domain, DKIM cryptographically signs the message, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when those checks fail and how to report
They scan attachments for ransomware inside the MTA, opening each MIME part and blocking delivery when the payload signature matches known malware
They replace TLS on SMTP submission (port 587), dropping STARTTLS and the certificate because the domain policy alone authenticates the channel to the relay
en.explanation: SPF authorizes sending hosts in a DNS TXT record. DKIM signs selected headers and the body with a domain key published in DNS. DMARC requires the visible From domain to align with SPF and/or DKIM and publishes a policy (none, quarantine, or reject) plus reporting. Together they fight domain spoofing; they do not encrypt the message and they do not replace SMTP TLS.

en.question: What is the main difference between EDR and XDR?
options: EDR only encrypts disks with a volume key on the endpoint; XDR only configures access VLANs on the switches, without collecting process, file, or host-behavior telemetry or correlating alerts from other security tools

They are the same product; XDR is just the Cisco name for the same antivirus signature file that EDR applies on the host, without correlating network, email, identity, or cloud telemetry in a single console
EDR replaces the perimeter firewall for traffic filtering; XDR replaces recursive DNS for name resolution, itself answering the A and AAAA queries made by internal clients instead of the resolver

EDR focuses on endpoint telemetry and response (processes, files, and host behavior); XDR correlates that with other sources such as network, email, identity, and cloud for a wider detection and response picture
en.explanation: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) collects telemetry and supports response on endpoints. XDR (Extended Detection and Response) extends detection and response across control points, correlating endpoint data with network, email, cloud, and identity. Cisco XDR is an example of that broader model. Neither one, by itself, replaces the firewall or disk encryption.

en.question: What is a SOAR platform mainly used for?
options: Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response: playbooks that automate and coordinate response steps across tools (tickets, firewall blocks, and enrichment)
A routing protocol that replaces OSPF in the data center, exchanging LSAs between spines and leaves to compute the shortest path and install it in the local RIB
A physical safe for storing firewall passwords, with a mechanical lock, a paper log, and a seal in the rack of the management consoles
A standard that forces every packet to be mirrored to one SPAN port on the campus aggregation switch, with no capture filter applied
en.explanation: SOAR (orchestration, automation, and response) runs playbooks: enrich alerts, open cases, isolate hosts, block indicators, and notify teams. It complements a SIEM, which detects and stores events, rather than replacing routing or SPAN.

en.question: In a security operations team, what is threat hunting?
options: Waiting only for high-severity SIEM alerts and closing them without looking for related activity on the endpoint, the network, or the identity logs during that same time window
Turning off firewall, endpoint, and DNS logging so an attacker cannot tell they were detected, deleting the telemetry at the collector before any SOC analyst is able to query it
A proactive search through telemetry for adversary activity that automated detections may have missed, often guided by a hypothesis and by frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK
Replacing every preventive control (firewall, MFA, patching) with a weekly manual log review, without filtering traffic, without requiring a second factor, and without applying fixes
en.explanation: Threat hunting assumes some intrusions evade alerts. Hunters form a hypothesis (for example a technique from ATT&CK), query endpoint, network, or identity data, and turn findings into new detections. It complements SIEM and EDR; it does not replace prevention and it does not mean ignoring alerts.

en.question: What is the main difference between an Indicator of Compromise (IoC) and an Indicator of Attack (IoA)?
options: IoCs are used only on physical security badges and door-reader inventories at the lobby, while IoAs are used only during wireless site surveys and RF heat maps that place access points on a floor plan

An IoC is typically a forensic artifact that suggests a compromise already happened (hash, IP, domain, file path), whereas an IoA focuses on behaviors/TTPs that show an attack is in progress—even before classic IoCs appear
IoAs replace CVE identifiers in public vulnerability databases, while IoCs replace the CVSS severity scores that patch-management teams use when they rank remediation work each week
There is no difference: vendors use the two terms interchangeably for the same firewall ACL entry that blocks one known-bad IP address or one known-bad domain name
en.explanation: IoCs are observable artifacts tied to known badness after or during compromise (malware hashes, C2 IPs/domains, filenames). IoAs emphasize attacker behaviors and techniques (e.g., unusual PowerShell, credential dumping patterns) so defenders can detect activity earlier and more resiliently when attackers change infrastructure. They are not badge/wireless concepts, not CVE/CVSS substitutes, and not synonymous ACL lines.

en.question: In a breach scenario, what does “lateral movement” usually mean?
options: Moving the data center racks sideways in the row to improve cooling airflow after an incident, without changing any compromised host, account, or internal network path
Rotating VPN certificates every hour so remote users must re-authenticate continuously, even when no host inside the network has been compromised by an attacker
After initial access, the attacker pivots from the first compromised host to other systems/accounts inside the network to expand control and reach high-value targets
Automatically failing over traffic from the primary ISP to a backup circuit when BGP withdraws a prefix, which is a routing event rather than a step inside an intrusion
en.explanation: Lateral movement is the post-compromise phase where adversaries hop between hosts and escalate or reuse credentials (RDP, SMB, Pass-the-Hash, remote management tools, etc.) to broaden foothold and reach crown jewels. It is not physical rack relocation, certificate rotation policy alone, or ISP failover.

en.question: What is a CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) primarily used for?
options: Sitting between users and cloud services to enforce security policy—visibility, compliance, data protection, and threat defense for SaaS/IaaS usage (including shadow IT)
Replacing the corporate core switch with a cloud-managed Layer 2-only fabric that cannot run OSPF, BGP, or any other routing protocol between the network closets
Generating CVSS severity scores automatically from NetFlow samples alone, without a vulnerability database, an asset inventory, or any scanner findings to score
Terminating all MPLS labels at the CASB so branch routers no longer need a provider edge and can drop their LDP or segment-routing sessions entirely
en.explanation: A Cloud Access Security Broker is a control point (API-based, reverse/forward proxy, or both) that applies enterprise security policy to cloud app usage: discover shadow IT, enforce DLP/access controls, and detect threats in SaaS/IaaS contexts. It is not a core-switch replacement, not a CVSS engine fed by NetFlow alone, and not an MPLS PE substitute.

en.question: How does Business Email Compromise (BEC) typically differ from classic mass phishing?
options: BEC always depends on zero-day browser exploits delivered in drive-by downloads, while phishing campaigns only ever use SMS text messages
BEC is a ransomware family that encrypts corporate mailboxes for payment, while phishing only steals guest Wi-Fi PSK passphrases from home routers
BEC is targeted social-engineering fraud (often fake execs/vendors) to divert money or data, not a broad credential-harvest lure
BEC only succeeds against personal consumer Gmail inboxes, while phishing only succeeds against corporate Active Directory password prompts
en.explanation: BEC is typically a focused fraud: attackers impersonate a CEO, finance lead, or trusted vendor and push a wire-transfer or data change without necessarily dropping malware. Classic phishing casts a wide net to steal passwords or deliver payloads. BEC is not defined as zero-day-only, ransomware-of-mailboxes, or limited to Gmail vs AD.

en.question: What is the primary goal of Data Loss Prevention (DLP) controls?
options: To retire perimeter firewalls completely so that only endpoint antivirus engines inspect and allow all outbound application traffic from laptops
To detect and stop sensitive data leaving approved channels without authorization
To ZIP-encrypt every departmental file share overnight so that backup windows finish faster on the tape or object-storage jobs
To give each user a freshly randomized MAC address at login so Layer-2 campus switches cannot track devices between buildings
en.explanation: DLP policies identify sensitive content and enforce rules on email, web, endpoints, or cloud apps so regulated or secret data is not exfiltrated casually. It complements—not replaces—firewalls and AV. It is not backup compression and not daily MAC randomization.

en.question: What does Network Detection and Response (NDR) primarily focus on?
options: Only scanning employee laptops once a month for missing Windows security patches and then opening ITSM tickets
Only managing firewall change-request tickets in an ITSM queue without ever inspecting packets, flows, or session metadata
Only forcing DoH or DoT so recursive DNS resolvers never observe plaintext query names from corporate clients
Analyzing network traffic/metadata (often east-west too) to detect threats and aid response
en.explanation: NDR tools watch network behavior—flows, sessions, sometimes full packets—to spot C2, lateral movement, and anomalies, then help analysts respond. That is broader than monthly patch scans, ITSM ticket hygiene alone, or DNS encryption (DoH/DoT), which are different controls.

en.question: What does UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) mainly look for?
options: Only the exact CVSS base score of every CVE published that calendar day, ignoring how accounts actually behave in production
Deviations from normal user and entity baselines that may signal compromise or insider misuse
Replacing every firewall ACL with a single any-any permit so analytics never observes blocked flows at the edge
Encrypting all syslog with one static pre-shared key and discarding every identity context coming from SSO
en.explanation: UEBA builds behavioral baselines for users and entities (hosts, service accounts) and flags anomalous activity that may indicate account takeover, insider threat, or lateral movement. It is not a CVE scoring feed, not an excuse to open firewalls to any-any, and not about discarding identity context from logs.

en.question: What is “shadow IT” in an enterprise security context?
options: The official CMDB inventory of every approved data-center rack plus its Cisco TAC serial numbers kept on file for audits
A mandatory quarterly tabletop exercise that only tests physical badge readers at the lobby turnstiles during drills
Business units adopting unsanctioned apps or cloud services outside IT governance and security review
A failover dark-fiber path used only by core switches during scheduled overnight maintenance windows on weekends
en.explanation: Shadow IT is the use of applications, SaaS, or infrastructure without IT/security approval—creating visibility, compliance, and data-leak gaps. It is not the official CMDB, not a lobby badge drill, and not a maintenance dark-fiber path.

en.question: What is an MFA fatigue (MFA bombing) attack trying to achieve?
options: Replace every corporate VPN concentrator with an open guest SSID that has no captive portal, no WPA, and no logging of associations at the edge
Downgrade all Internet TLS sessions to cleartext HTTP by flooding only ICMP echo requests toward every recursive resolver on the campus DNS farm
Flood the user with push/OTP prompts until they approve one out of annoyance, giving the attacker a session
Erase every BGP community on all edge routers overnight so traffic-engineering tags can never be matched by any route-map again in production
en.explanation: MFA fatigue/bombing overwhelms the legitimate user with authentication prompts so they eventually accept one, handing the attacker an authenticated session after credential theft or password spray. It is not about open guest SSIDs as the mechanism, ICMP-only TLS downgrade, or clearing BGP communities.

en.question: What does a basic container escape mean for a host running Docker/Kubernetes workloads?
options: The container process only loses its IPv4 address and must renew DHCP on eth0, with no change at all to isolation boundaries or host privileges
Attacker/malware breaks container isolation and can affect the host or sibling containers
Kubernetes always converts every Pod into a full Type-1 hypervisor VM that cannot share a kernel with the worker node under any CNI plugin
Escape only renames the Docker bridge interface to VLAN 1 and disables every NetworkPolicy object in the cluster automatically without RBAC checks
en.explanation: A container escape is when code inside a container breaks isolation (namespaces/cgroups/capabilities/misconfig) and reaches the host OS or sibling workloads. It is not a harmless DHCP renew, not a claim that every Pod becomes a Type-1 VM, and not merely renaming a Docker bridge.

en.question: What problem does certificate (public-key) pinning mainly try to reduce in a mobile or thick client app?
options: It forces every access-switch port into err-disabled whenever a user installs a corporate root CA on their laptop for mail or VPN enrollment
It replaces enterprise DNS entirely with static /etc/hosts files on every endpoint so apps never resolve names through recursive resolvers again
It stores the user's reusable password inside the leaf certificate Subject CN field so MFA prompts are never required after the first login
It limits which server certs/keys the app trusts, reducing some TLS MITM with unexpected CAs
en.explanation: Certificate pinning (or public-key pinning) teaches the client to expect a specific cert or key (or small set), so a TLS proxy presenting a different CA-signed cert is more likely to fail. It does not err-disable switch ports, replace DNS with hosts files, or embed passwords in certificate CNs.

en.question: What does microsegmentation mainly aim to control for east-west traffic inside a data center or cloud VPC?
options: Replace every border firewall with a single hub switch so all tenants share one flat VLAN and one default gateway forever
Limit lateral movement by enforcing fine-grained allow rules between workloads, not only at the north-south perimeter
Turn off all encryption between VMs so packet brokers can mirror every east-west flow without TLS inspection licenses
Force every database query to travel over dial-up modems while web tiers may only use token-ring bridges from the 1990s
en.explanation: Microsegmentation applies identity- or label-based controls between workloads so a breach in one app tier cannot freely reach others (east-west). It complements, not replaces, perimeter controls. It is not about flattening all tenants onto one VLAN, disabling encryption for taps, or using obsolete dial-up/token-ring paths.

en.question: What does a living-off-the-land (LOLBins) technique mainly rely on during an intrusion?
options: Shipping a brand-new unsigned kernel driver on every USB stick left in the parking lot so defenders only look for foreign binaries
Replacing the corporate DNS root with a public NTP pool so every laptop loses its default gateway until reimaging
Abusing trusted built-in OS tools (PowerShell, wmic, bash, certutil) already on the host instead of dropping obvious malware files
Disabling every firewall rule worldwide via a single SNMP write to the core so lateral movement never needs credentials again
en.explanation: Living-off-the-land abuses legitimate, preinstalled binaries and scripts so malicious actions blend with admin activity and may evade simple file-hash AV. It is not defined by USB kernel drivers alone, DNS/NTP pranks, or a magic SNMP write that opens the whole internet.

en.question: In a software supply-chain compromise (SolarWinds-style), what trust relationship is the attacker mainly abusing?
options: A trusted vendor update or build pipeline so malicious code rides signed software that customers already allow
Only the guest Wi-Fi captive portal so attackers can print cafeteria coupons while never touching production build servers
The office coffee machine’s Bluetooth beacon so it rewrites BGP communities on every PE router each morning before lunch
A single unused lobby fax line that somehow becomes the organization’s only public certificate authority overnight
en.explanation: Supply-chain attacks target the trust customers place in vendor updates or CI/CD artifacts—malware is injected upstream and delivered as “legitimate” software. Guest Wi-Fi portals, coffee-machine Bluetooth, and lobby fax lines are not the defining abuse path for this class of attack.

en.question: What is the main security purpose of deploying honeypots or broader deception technology?
options: To permanently replace every production firewall rule with an open any-any policy so attackers never need to scan the network again
To store all employee passwords in a single cleartext spreadsheet that auditors can download freely without completing any MFA challenge
To place decoy systems or credentials that attract attackers, raise high-confidence alerts, and waste adversary time without real data
To disable logging on every domain controller so lateral movement becomes invisible to the SOC for the rest of the engagement entirely
en.explanation: Honeypots/deception present fake assets or tokens that legitimate users rarely touch; interaction is a strong signal of hostile activity and can delay or distract attackers. They do not open firewalls any-any, store passwords in cleartext, or disable DC logging.

en.question: Why do attackers sometimes abuse DNS tunneling for command-and-control or data exfiltration?
options: Because DNS queries/responses can carry encoded payloads and often pass perimeter filters that allow DNS, hiding C2 or stolen data
Because DNS always encrypts every payload with TLS 1.3 end-to-end and therefore cannot be inspected by any resolver or firewall device
Because DNS replaces BGP on the Internet backbone and routers forward stolen files only as OSPF Type-5 external LSAs worldwide
Because disabling the recursive resolver permanently deletes every Active Directory account without leaving any audit log entries
en.explanation: DNS tunneling encodes data in DNS queries/answers; many networks permit DNS outbound, so it can bypass controls that block other protocols. DNS is not inherently TLS-encrypted end-to-end for all queries, does not replace BGP/OSPF, and does not wipe AD accounts.

en.question: In disaster recovery planning, how do RTO and RPO mainly differ?
options: RTO is only the brand of the backup tape library; RPO is the Wi-Fi channel number used during quarterly on-site failover drills
RTO and RPO are identical metrics that always equal the OSPF Dead interval configured on the WAN edge router pair in production
RTO measures how long the SOC may retain phishing emails; RPO measures how many firewall rules must be deleted each night forever
RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage; RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss looking backward
en.explanation: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) limits how long a service may stay down; Recovery Point Objective (RPO) limits how much data you can afford to lose, expressed as time before the incident. They are not tape brands, OSPF timers, or phishing/firewall housekeeping metrics.

en.question: In a Windows Active Directory environment, what does a pass-the-hash (PtH) attack mainly reuse?
options: Only the cleartext password typed once at the keyboard, never any stored credential material from memory or databases
A stolen NTLM (or similar) password hash to authenticate as the user without knowing the cleartext password
A forged BGP UPDATE that injects a more-specific route so all domain controllers become unreachable from the LAN
A rogue DHCP server that hands out an APIPA range so clients lose DNS and cannot locate the domain controllers
en.explanation: Pass-the-hash reuses captured NTLM (or related) hashes to authenticate without cracking the cleartext password. It is not limited to one typed cleartext password, and it is not a BGP or rogue-DHCP technique.

en.question: What is the main security purpose of planting canary tokens (or similar honeytokens) in files, URLs, or credentials?
options: To replace the corporate SIEM entirely so analysts no longer need logs, alerts, or correlation rules of any kind
To encrypt every endpoint disk with a unique BitLocker key derived only from the canary string and the hostname
To get a high-confidence alert when someone accesses a fake resource that legitimate users should never touch
To permanently disable MFA for privileged accounts so operators can log in faster during a declared incident
en.explanation: Canary tokens / honeytokens are decoy artifacts that should not be used in normal work; access triggers a strong signal of probing or theft. They do not replace SIEM, encrypt disks by themselves, or disable MFA.

en.question: What does an air-gapped system mainly rely on for isolation from remote network threats?
options: Physical (or strictly controlled) separation from untrusted networks so remote malware cannot reach it over IP
A single public cloud VPC with open security groups so operators can patch faster from any Internet host
Always-on site-to-site IPsec to the Internet edge so every update is pulled automatically without review
Disabling local logging and antivirus so the host uses fewer CPU cycles while still joining the corporate Wi-Fi
en.explanation: Air-gapping isolates a system by keeping it off untrusted networks (physically or with extreme controls), reducing remote malware and C2 paths. Open cloud exposure, always-on Internet IPsec, or joining corporate Wi-Fi while disabling defenses contradicts that isolation goal.

en.question: How do red team, blue team, and purple team roles mainly differ in a security exercise?
options: Red team only writes compliance policies and audit checklists; blue team only patches firmware; purple team only manages physical badges at the door
Blue team simulates external attackers end-to-end; red team only monitors SIEM alerts; purple team disables logging to reduce noise during tests
Red team emulates attackers; blue team defends and detects; purple team improves collaboration so offense findings raise defense quality
All three names mean the same SOC tier and only differ by which vendor logo appears on the shared ticketing and dashboard screens
en.explanation: Red teams emulate adversaries (offense). Blue teams protect, detect, and respond (defense). Purple teaming bridges them so attack techniques and detections improve together. The other options reverse or invent duties and wrongly treat the labels as identical SOC tiers.

en.question: What is the main difference between consuming threat intelligence feeds and doing threat hunting?
options: Feeds only list approved software versions for patch Tuesday windows; hunting only inventories printers, so neither activity uses network telemetry at all
Threat intel feeds deliver indicators or context to enrich detection; threat hunting proactively searches telemetry for threats that may lack prior alerts
Hunting replaces all feeds because a hunter never uses IOCs in practice; feeds replace hunting because automation alone closes every unknown intrusion case
Feeds are only for red teams during phishing drills and tabletop games; hunting is only for HR background checks and never touches security logs or packets
en.explanation: Threat intelligence feeds supply IOCs/TTPs/context that tools and analysts can use. Threat hunting is a proactive search through telemetry for suspicious activity that alerting may have missed. Hunting often uses intel, but it is not the same as passively ingesting feeds; neither activity is limited to patch lists, printers, or HR checks.

en.question: What does a Kerberoasting attack mainly try to obtain in an Active Directory environment?
options: Cleartext VPN pre-shared keys from the DHCP options field by spoofing a rogue helper-address on every access VLAN in the campus
Offline-crackable service account password material by requesting service tickets for SPNs and extracting ticket hashes
A permanent golden certificate for MDM enrollment by replaying WPA3 SAE handshakes captured only on the guest Wi-Fi SSID segment
Root SSH private keys from network devices by forcing all BGP sessions to fall back to TCP-AO with an intentionally empty keychain
en.explanation: Kerberoasting requests Kerberos service tickets (TGS) for accounts with SPNs, extracts the encrypted material, and cracks it offline to recover service-account passwords—often highly privileged. It is not about DHCP helper spoofing for VPN PSKs, WPA3 SAE golden MDM certs, or emptying BGP TCP-AO keychains for SSH roots.

en.question: What does an NTLM relay attack mainly try to abuse in a Windows environment?
options: It cracks Kerberos TGTs offline by capturing AS-REP responses only from accounts that have Kerberos pre-authentication explicitly disabled in the domain
It captures a victim’s NTLM authentication attempt and relays it to another service so the attacker can authenticate as that user without knowing the password
It floods RADIUS with forged EAP-TLS client certificates until the NPS server revokes every machine account and computer object stored in Active Directory today
It only turns off SMB signing on the attacker’s own laptop so local disk images open slightly faster during routine forensic acquisition of spare drives
en.explanation: NTLM relay intercepts a legitimate NTLM authentication and reuses it against a different target (often when signing or channel-binding protections are weak). It is not AS-REP roasting, not EAP-TLS flooding of RADIUS, and not a local SMB performance tweak.

en.question: How does password spraying mainly differ from a classic online brute-force attack against one account?
options: Spraying only works against SSH public keys and never against web portals, VPN gateways, or other login forms that still accept ordinary user passwords
Spraying requires physical console access to the domain controller so every guessed password can be written directly into the NTDS.dit database file on disk
Spraying tries a small set of common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts, while classic brute force hammers many passwords against one target account
There is no real difference: both names describe the same Kerberoasting workflow that requests service tickets and cracks their hashes completely offline afterward
en.explanation: Password spraying spreads a few likely passwords across many users to stay under account-lockout thresholds; classic online brute force focuses many guesses on one account. It is not limited to SSH keys, does not need DC console access, and is not Kerberoasting.

en.question: In Active Directory attacks, what does a successful DCSync mainly allow an adversary to do?
options: Abuse domain-controller replication rights to pull password hashes (for example via DRSUAPI) from AD without executing payload code on the DC’s interactive console
Replace every Group Policy administrative template with a malicious MSI so all workstations install unwanted software during the next mandatory reboot maintenance window
Disable Kerberos authentication for the entire forest and force every interactive and network logon to use only NTLMv1 with no fallback to newer protocols
Rewrite all user SPNs into public DNS CNAME records so ticket-granting tickets are resolved only through external recursive resolvers on the Internet
en.explanation: DCSync abuses directory replication privileges (often after stealing high-privilege credentials) to request account secrets/hashes as if the attacker were a DC. It is not about swapping GPO MSI packages, turning off Kerberos forest-wide, or rewriting SPNs into public DNS CNAMEs.

en.question: In malware analysis, what does “sandbox detonation” mainly mean?
options: Wiping the production domain controller overnight so every suspicious binary is forced to reinstall itself from a USB stick on the next reboot of every joined workstation
Disabling all EDR sensors for 24 hours so analysts can copy malware hashes directly into the live Active Directory schema and Group Policy templates
Running a suspicious file in an isolated virtual environment to observe behavior (network, file, registry) without infecting production hosts
Publishing the full sample to a public paste site so every SOC worldwide can recompile the binary before any local static or dynamic analysis starts
en.explanation: Sandbox detonation executes a suspect sample in a controlled isolated environment to capture behavioral indicators safely. It is not wiping DCs, disabling EDR to touch AD schema, or dumping samples to public paste sites as the definition.

en.question: In Active Directory attacks, how does a Golden Ticket mainly differ from a Silver Ticket?
options: A Golden Ticket is only valid on Linux workstations joined via Samba, while a Silver Ticket works exclusively on Azure AD cloud-only tenants without any on-premises domain controller present
A Golden Ticket forges a TGT with the KRBTGT hash for broad service-ticket requests; a Silver Ticket forges a TGS for one service using that service account’s hash
Both tickets are identical JWT tokens issued by Entra ID Conditional Access policies and never involve Kerberos keys stored on on-premises domain controllers at all
A Silver Ticket always requires DCSync rights first on a DC, whereas a Golden Ticket can be minted from any local guest account without domain credentials or KRBTGT material
en.explanation: Golden Tickets forge TGTs with the KRBTGT hash (broad access to request service tickets). Silver Tickets forge a TGS for one service using that service’s account hash. They are Kerberos constructs, not Linux-only/Azure-only JWT rules, and Silver does not uniquely require DCSync first.

en.question: In network detection, what does malware “beaconing” to a C2 (command-and-control) server typically look like?
options: A single burst of random UDP noise that never repeats and only appears during the first DHCP Discover after a cold boot of the endpoint on the access VLAN
Continuous full-mesh OSPF flooding between every workstation so the C2 can rewrite the campus IGP topology and area types in real time across all sites
Encrypted emails sent only to the local mail gateway that contain no callbacks and never open outbound connections to any external host or resolver
Periodic, often low-and-slow outbound connections or DNS queries from an implant back to attacker infrastructure to check in and receive commands
en.explanation: Beaconing is repeated check-ins from malware to C2 (HTTP/DNS/etc.), often periodic and stealthy. It is not a one-shot DHCP UDP burst, OSPF mesh rewriting, or email-only traffic with no outbound callbacks.

en.question: What does AS-REP roasting mainly abuse in Active Directory Kerberos environments?
options: It floods RADIUS with EAP-TLS handshakes until every wireless controller forgets its AAA servers and falls back to open SSIDs across the entire campus fabric
It rewrites BGP communities on all PE routers overnight so return traffic prefers a malicious ISP peer that advertises only a default route into the enterprise
It empties every DHCP pool by spoofing Discover storms with random MACs so clients receive only APIPA addresses and never learn the domain DNS servers
It requests AS-REP messages for accounts that do not require Kerberos pre-authentication, then cracks the encrypted material offline to recover those passwords
en.explanation: AS-REP roasting targets accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled: the attacker obtains AS-REP ciphertext and cracks it offline for the account password. It is not a RADIUS/EAP-TLS flood, BGP community rewrite, or DHCP starvation technique.

en.question: In Kerberos-based attacks, what does Pass-the-Ticket (PtT) mainly involve?
options: Cracking NTLM challenge-response pairs captured only from LLMNR/NBT-NS spoofing on the LAN, without ever reading or injecting a Kerberos ticket from any cache
Sending phishing SMS one-time codes that expire in thirty seconds so MFA fatigue forces every user to approve a rogue push notification on their phone
Reusing a stolen Kerberos ticket (TGT or service ticket) from memory or disk to authenticate as that principal without knowing the account password
Brute-forcing WPA3 SAE handshakes offline for days to mint a permanent MDM enrollment certificate that works only on guest SSIDs and never on corporate SSIDs
en.explanation: Pass-the-Ticket reuses a stolen Kerberos ticket (often from LSASS/ticket cache) to authenticate without the cleartext password. It is distinct from NTLM hash cracking via LLMNR spoofing, MFA-fatigue phishing, or WPA3 SAE cracking.

en.question: Why do attackers often dump credentials from the LSASS process on a Windows host?
options: LSASS only stores printer spooler queue names and driver paths, so dumping it is required before any lateral movement over SMB can begin on the corporate LAN segment
LSASS holds authentication material (e.g., NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, sometimes cleartext) that can enable Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, or further domain pivots
LSASS is the only place Group Policy stores Wi-Fi PSKs for every SSID, and dumping it replaces the need for any domain credentials when joining cloud-only Azure AD tenants
LSASS encrypts the local BIOS firmware image each boot, so dumping it is the only supported way to unlock BitLocker recovery keys from the TPM PCR banks on that host
en.explanation: LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) caches logon secrets such as NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets; dumping it fuels PtH/PtT and lateral movement. It is not a printer-queue store, not the sole GPO Wi-Fi PSK vault for Azure join, and not a BIOS/BitLocker TPM unlock ritual.

en.question: What characterizes fileless malware in endpoint attacks?
options: It runs mainly in memory or via trusted built-in tools/scripts (e.g., PowerShell, WMI) with little or no traditional malicious EXE written to disk, making file-based AV scans less effective

It can only infect air-gapped printers that lack any CPU, RAM, or network stack, and it always stores a full PE binary under C:\Windows\System32 before every execution, regardless of any vendor-specific default on the platform.

It is defined as any USB autorun worm that requires the victim to double-click a .exe on a mapped network drive and never uses living-off-the-land binaries or in-memory techniques in typical campus and enterprise production networks alike.

It exclusively encrypts disk partitions with a public ransomware note and never abuses scripting hosts, registry-resident payloads, or reflective DLL injection in memory across common IOS, IOS-XE, and NX-OS deployment models.
en.explanation: Fileless malware favors memory-resident or living-off-the-land execution (PowerShell/WMI/etc.) so classic on-disk signature scanning struggles. It is not limited to air-gapped printers, not defined as USB-only EXE worms, and not synonymous with ransomware-only disk encryption.

en.question: In cyber threat scenarios, what does island hopping typically describe?
options: Physically moving hard drives between two air-gapped data centers over a courier route that never uses the Internet or any managed service provider network, regardless of any vendor-specific default on the platform.
Compromising a weaker connected organization (often a supplier/MSP/partner) and then pivoting from that trusted relationship into the primary target’s environment

Jumping VLANs only by forging 802.1Q tags on a local switch port without ever phishing, exploiting, or abusing any third-party trust path outside the LAN in typical campus and enterprise production networks alike.
Rotating C2 domains every millisecond with a cryptographic one-time pad so that DNS resolvers and TLS SNI inspection become permanently impossible on every path
en.explanation: Island hopping abuses trust in a connected third party (supplier/MSP/partner): breach the weaker island, then pivot into the real target. It is not courier air-gap disk moves, not pure local VLAN hopping, and not a definition of ultra-fast C2 domain rotation.

en.question: How do Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) commonly help malware maintain command-and-control reachability?
options: They permanently pin a single hard-coded IP in the binary so defenders only ever need to block one address for the lifetime of the campaign with no DNS involvement, regardless of any vendor-specific default on the platform.

They replace every DNS query with static /etc/hosts entries distributed by USB so the malware never contacts a resolver and cannot be observed in passive DNS telemetry in typical campus and enterprise production networks alike.
They algorithmically generate many candidate domain names over time; the operator registers one (or a few) in that set so infected hosts can still find C2 even after individual domains are blocked

They encrypt the entire OSPF LSDB inside TXT records so routers treat botnet traffic as Type-5 externals and never allow security teams to sinkhole any generated name across common IOS, IOS-XE, and NX-OS deployment models.
en.explanation: DGAs produce many possible domain names; attackers register the ones they need so malware can rediscover C2 after takedowns. They are not single hard-coded IPs, not USB /etc/hosts-only, and not OSPF LSDB-in-TXT tricks.

en.question: What is server-side request forgery (SSRF)?
options: An attack where a script injected into a web page runs in other users' browsers and steals their session cookies while they view the page
An attack where a victim's browser is tricked into sending an authenticated request to a site they are logged into, such as changing a password
An attack where the attacker makes a vulnerable server send requests to targets of their choice, such as internal services or cloud metadata endpoints
An attack where the attacker floods a web server with half-open TCP connections until its connection table is completely full and new users cannot connect
en.explanation: In SSRF the server itself is abused as a proxy, often to reach internal-only systems or cloud metadata (e.g., 169.254.169.254) and steal credentials. Option 1 describes XSS, option 2 CSRF (client-side forgery), and option 4 a SYN flood.

en.question: How does domain fronting help malware hide its command-and-control (C2) traffic?
options: It registers thousands of random domains every day so that the defenders cannot block all of them before the malware finds one that the operator controls
It rewrites the DNS records of the victim's own domain so that internal users are redirected to a cloned login page that is hosted by the attacker
It hides C2 commands inside ICMP echo payloads so that firewalls that only inspect TCP and UDP traffic never see the attacker's instructions at all
It shows a reputable CDN-hosted domain in DNS and the TLS SNI, while the HTTP Host header inside the encrypted session points to the attacker's backend
en.explanation: Domain fronting abuses CDNs: the visible layers (DNS, SNI) name a trusted domain, but the inner Host header routes the request to the attacker's service on the same CDN, so blocking it means blocking the popular domain. Option 1 is DGA, option 2 DNS hijacking/pharming, and option 3 ICMP tunneling.

en.question: During incident response, which evidence should normally be collected first according to the order of volatility?
options: CPU registers, cache and RAM contents, along with running processes and live network connections, because they are lost at shutdown
Archived backup tapes stored offsite, because they are the oldest copies of the data and are the most likely to be overwritten first
The full hard disk image of the affected host, because disk data disappears as soon as the incident responder opens the case ticket
Printed logs and physical documents in the office, because paper evidence degrades faster than any data held in the system memory
en.explanation: The order of volatility says to capture the most short-lived data first: registers, cache, RAM, process and network state, then temporary files, disk, remote logs and finally archival media. Backups and disk images are far less volatile than memory.

en.question: An attacker loads a bank's transfer page inside an invisible iframe on a game site and tricks users into clicking a hidden Confirm button. What is this attack and a standard defense?
options: Clickjacking; the bank should send X-Frame-Options DENY or CSP frame-ancestors so browsers refuse to render its pages in frames
Cross-site scripting; the bank should hash every password with bcrypt so injected scripts can no longer read the stored credentials
SQL injection; the bank should use parameterized queries so the hidden button cannot change the SQL statement sent to its database
DNS spoofing; the bank should enable DNSSEC on its zone so the game site can no longer resolve the bank's domain to a rogue server
en.explanation: Clickjacking (UI redressing) overlays a framed legitimate page under a decoy so the victim clicks real buttons. The fix is to forbid framing with X-Frame-Options or Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors. No script is injected, no SQL is altered and DNS resolution is untouched.

en.question: A malicious site's domain first resolves to the attacker's server with a very short TTL, then re-resolves to 192.168.1.1, letting the victim's browser send requests to the home router's admin page. What is this technique?
options: DNS cache poisoning, because the attacker injects forged answers into the ISP resolver so every user of that resolver is redirected to the router
Domain generation algorithm (DGA), because the malware creates thousands of random domains per day so defenders cannot block its servers
DNS rebinding, because the same origin is rebound to an internal IP, so the browser's same-origin policy lets the attacker's script reach it
DNS tunneling, because the attacker encodes stolen data in long subdomain labels and exfiltrates it through normal recursive DNS queries
en.explanation: DNS rebinding abuses short TTLs: the hostname (same origin) is switched to a private IP, so the attacker's JavaScript can talk to internal devices. Defenses include resolvers blocking private answers for public names, Host-header checks and authentication on internal services. Cache poisoning forges resolver data, DGA is for C2 resilience and tunneling is for exfiltration.

en.question: A company's build server pulls an internal package named acme-utils. An attacker publishes acme-utils version 99.0 on the public npm registry, and the build installs it. What is this attack and a key mitigation?
options: Typosquatting; developers should be trained to spell package names carefully, because the attack only works when a name is mistyped
Dependency confusion; use scoped or namespaced packages and point the build at a private registry with pinned versions and lockfiles
Watering hole attack; block the npm website on the corporate proxy, since the package is only delivered to users browsing the registry
Man-in-the-browser; install an anti-malware extension on build agents, because the malicious code is injected into the browser session
en.explanation: Dependency confusion exploits package managers that prefer the highest version across public and private sources. Scopes/namespaces, a single private registry (proxying public), version pinning and lockfiles prevent it. Typosquatting relies on misspelled names, a watering hole compromises a site victims visit, and man-in-the-browser is browser-session malware.

en.question: A logged-in user changes the URL /api/invoices/1043 to /api/invoices/1044 and sees another customer's invoice. Which vulnerability is this?
options: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF), because the browser sends the session cookie with a request that the user never meant to send
Directory traversal, because the number in the path lets the user climb out of the web root and read files from the server disk
Insecure direct object reference (IDOR), a broken access control flaw where the server does not check who owns the record
Session fixation, because the attacker set the session ID before login and can now reuse it to read the other customer's data
en.explanation: IDOR (part of OWASP Broken Access Control) happens when the app trusts an object ID from the client without checking that the logged-in user may access it. The fix is a server-side authorization check on every object (random IDs alone are not enough). CSRF forges requests from the victim's browser, traversal uses ../ to reach files and session fixation reuses a pre-set session ID.

en.question: Users with push-notification MFA are phished through a reverse proxy that shows the real Microsoft 365 login page. The attacker then signs in without any MFA prompt. What happened, and what resists it best?
options: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing stole the session cookie after MFA; phishing-resistant FIDO2/passkeys bound to the origin stop it
MFA fatigue flooded users with push prompts until one was approved; number matching on the prompts is enough to stop this reverse proxy
SIM swapping moved the users' phone numbers to the attacker; switching from SMS codes to push notifications fully blocks the attack
Password spraying guessed common passwords; a longer lockout threshold on accounts prevents the attacker from reusing the session
en.explanation: AiTM kits (e.g. Evilginx) relay the real login, so the victim completes MFA and the proxy captures the session cookie, which the attacker replays. FIDO2/passkeys are bound to the real domain and will not sign for the proxy's domain; conditional access and token binding also help. MFA fatigue needs repeated prompts, SIM swapping targets SMS and spraying only guesses passwords.

en.question: An employee clicks a link and approves an app called 'PDF Viewer' that asks for Mail.Read and offline_access in Microsoft 365. Later, mail is read even after the employee's password is reset. What is this?
options: Credential stuffing, because the attacker reused a leaked password from another site and a password reset does not end it
Cookie theft by malware, because the infostealer copied browser cookies that stay valid for the mailbox after a reset
Typosquatting, because the employee went to a lookalike domain and the fake site keeps reading mail through webmail
Illicit consent grant (OAuth consent phishing); the app holds its own refresh token, so the consent must be revoked
en.explanation: In consent phishing the attacker never needs the password: the user grants a malicious OAuth app delegated permissions, and offline_access gives it a refresh token that survives a password reset. Fix it by revoking the app's consent and tokens and restricting user consent to verified publishers or admin approval. Credential stuffing and stolen cookies are cut off by a reset with session revocation, and typosquatting is just a lookalike domain.

en.question: A login form builds SQL with string concatenation from the username field. Which defense best stops classic SQL injection here?
options: Rely on a WAF signature set alone, because modern WAFs rewrite every query before it reaches the database engine
Hash the username with SHA-256 before concatenation, so injected quotes become hex and cannot close the string
Switch the column to a numeric ID only and keep concatenating, because numbers cannot carry SQL metacharacters
Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) so user input is bound as data and never parsed as SQL code
en.explanation: Parameterized queries / prepared statements separate the SQL statement from bound values, so input cannot change the query structure. WAFs help as defense-in-depth but miss novel payloads; hashing the username still leaves a concatenated query; numeric casting helps one field but is not a general fix and error-based tricks can remain.

en.question: On Windows, a service ImagePath is C:\Program Files\Vendor App\service.exe without quotes, and Authenticated Users can write to C:\Program Files\Vendor App\. How can a local attacker escalate to the service account?
options: Replace the system-wide PATH so cmd.exe runs first, because Windows always searches PATH before ImagePath folder entries on disk
Plant malware earlier on the unquoted path (e.g. C:\Program.exe) so the Service Control Manager launches it
Enable SeDebugPrivilege via whoami /priv and dump LSASS, which is required before any unquoted ImagePath can be abused
Clear the service's DependOnService list so Windows reinstalls the binary from an attacker-controlled UNC path at boot
en.explanation: Unquoted service paths with spaces make the Service Control Manager try C:\Program.exe, then C:\Program Files\Vendor.exe, then the real path. Write permission in an earlier folder lets an attacker drop a binary the SCM runs as the service identity (often LocalSystem). PATH hijacking is a different issue; SeDebug/LSASS dump is another technique; DependOnService does not reinstall from UNC that way.

en.question: Which statement best distinguishes stored XSS from reflected XSS in a typical web application?
options: Stored XSS only works over cleartext HTTP, while reflected XSS requires HTTPS plus a valid client certificate before any script can run in the browser
Stored XSS keeps the script in server data for later viewers; reflected XSS echoes the payload only in that immediate response
Stored XSS modifies only DNS records on the resolver, while reflected XSS rewrites ARP caches on the victim’s access switch
Stored XSS needs a malicious browser extension, while reflected XSS needs only a crafted email with no link the user opens
en.explanation: Stored (persistent) XSS saves the payload in an application store (comment, profile, ticket) so other users later receive and execute it. Reflected XSS takes the payload from the request and reflects it in that response (often via a malicious URL). Transport HTTP/HTTPS and client certs do not define the difference; neither XSS type is about DNS/ARP poisoning; extensions are unrelated to the classic classification.

en.question: A banking site relies on session cookies for authenticated POSTs. Which defense best stops classic CSRF on a state-changing transfer?
options: Disable TLS on the transfer endpoint so browsers refuse to send cookies on cross-site POSTs that lack an HTTPS URL
Hash the account number with MD5 in the JSON body, because CSRF tooling cannot forge that digest without the bank’s offline HSM private key material
Require a per-session anti-CSRF token (or SameSite=Strict cookies) so forged cross-site POSTs lack the expected secret
Open CORS with Access-Control-Allow-Origin * so the browser blocks credentialed cross-origin POSTs automatically
en.explanation: Classic CSRF uses the browser’s automatic cookie send on a forged cross-site request. Synchronizer/anti-CSRF tokens (or strict SameSite cookies) ensure the forged request lacks a secret only the legitimate app page can read. Disabling TLS does not stop cookie sends; MD5 of a public account number is not a CSRF secret; ACAO * does not block credentialed CSRF and is the opposite of a tight CORS policy.

en.question: Why is UEFI Secure Boot (or Measured Boot with TPM attestations) still useful even when the disk is fully encrypted with BitLocker-class FDE?
options: It protects boot-chain integrity so malware cannot replace the bootloader/kernel before the OS unlocks the encrypted volume
It replaces disk encryption entirely, because a validated bootloader already encrypts every file with the TPM endorsement key
It stops all phishing of cloud admin accounts by binding each HTTPS session to the platform’s Secure Boot database hash
It removes the need for OS patching, since only Microsoft-signed boot components can ever contain exploitable vulnerabilities
en.explanation: Full disk encryption protects confidentiality of data at rest, but a compromised bootloader or kernel can run before/during unlock and subvert the OS. Secure Boot verifies signatures on boot components; Measured Boot/attestation records hashes in the TPM for remote verification. FDE is not replaced by Secure Boot; Secure Boot does not stop phishing; signed boot code still needs patching and does not imply the whole OS is bug-free.

en.question: What does an XML External Entity (XXE) attack mainly abuse in a vulnerable parser?
options: It floods the DNS resolver with random subdomains generated by a DGA so recursive queries exhaust resolver cache memory space
It spoofs the victim’s MAC on the default gateway so ARP replies redirect HTTPS sessions into a local SSL strip proxy host
It tricks the parser into resolving external entities, which can read local files or reach internal URLs from the server
It replaces the UEFI bootloader signature database so Secure Boot accepts an unsigned kernel before BitLocker unlocks disk
en.explanation: XXE abuses XML parsers that process external entity references. A crafted document can make the server fetch file:// resources or internal HTTP URLs (often overlapping with SSRF-like impact). It is not a DGA DNS flood, not ARP spoofing, and not a Secure Boot/bootloader attack.

en.question: In Windows malware tradecraft, what does process hollowing mainly involve?
options: Encrypting only the Master Boot Record with a ransomware note while leaving user files in plaintext NTFS clusters
Starting a legitimate process suspended, unmapping its code, and injecting malicious code before it resumes
Registering a rogue DHCP server that hands out an attacker DNS so browsers resolve banks to phishing sites
Brute-forcing Kerberos AS-REP for users without pre-authentication to crack hashes offline without tickets
en.explanation: Process hollowing creates a legitimate process in a suspended state, hollows out (unmaps) its memory image, injects attacker code, then resumes so the malicious payload runs under a trusted process name. It is not MBR-only ransomware, not rogue DHCP/DNS, and not AS-REP roasting (a Kerberos pre-auth weakness).

en.question: What is Microsoft Sysmon mainly used for on Windows endpoints in a blue-team monitoring design?
options: It replaces Windows Defender real-time scanning by signing every executable with a local self-signed code-signing certificate
It is a full disk encryption feature that stores BitLocker recovery keys only in the TPM and never in Active Directory
It is a VPN client that forces all corporate traffic through WireGuard tunnels before any process can open a socket
It provides detailed process, network, and file-creation event logs that SIEM/EDR pipelines can use for detection
en.explanation: Sysmon (System Monitor) is a Windows system service/driver that logs rich telemetry—process creates, network connections, file/registry changes, and more—into the Windows event log for SIEM or detection engineering. It does not replace Defender AV, is not BitLocker, and is not a VPN client.

en.question: What does a typical WAF bypass attempt mainly try to achieve against a web application firewall?
options: It floods the recursive DNS resolver with random DGA subdomains until cache memory is exhausted on every resolver node
It crafts requests (encoding, alternate paths, verb tricks) so malicious payloads reach the app without matching WAF rules
It spoofs the default-gateway MAC address so forged ARP replies redirect HTTPS sessions into a local SSL-strip proxy host
It replaces the UEFI Secure Boot signature database so firmware accepts an unsigned bootloader before BitLocker unlocks disk
en.explanation: WAF bypasses abuse gaps between what the WAF normalizes/matches and what the backend app accepts—encodings, path confusion, HTTP verb/content-type tricks, and similar. It is not a DGA DNS flood, ARP spoofing, or Secure Boot attack.

en.question: In Windows tradecraft, what does DLL sideloading mainly involve?
options: Encrypting only the Master Boot Record with a ransomware note while leaving all user files in plaintext NTFS clusters
Registering a rogue DHCP server that hands out attacker-controlled DNS so browsers resolve banks to phishing landing pages
Placing a malicious DLL where a trusted signed app will load it by search order, running attacker code in that process
Brute-forcing Kerberos AS-REP for accounts without pre-authentication so hashes can be cracked offline without any tickets
en.explanation: DLL sideloading abuses how Windows apps resolve DLL paths: an attacker drops a malicious DLL that a legitimate signed binary loads, often to blend into trusted processes and bypass simple application allow-lists. It is not MBR-only ransomware, rogue DHCP/DNS, or AS-REP roasting.

en.question: In Active Directory, why is unconstrained Kerberos delegation considered especially dangerous if an attacker compromises that host?
options: The host can reuse tickets of users who authenticate to it to impersonate them toward other services across the domain
It disables Kerberos completely and forces every interactive logon to use plaintext LDAP simple binds on TCP port 389 only
It converts all service accounts into Domain Admins automatically after the next Group Policy refresh interval completes
It stores BitLocker recovery keys inside SYSVOL in cleartext so any Authenticated User can read them from the share
en.explanation: With unconstrained delegation, a computer/service receives and can forward TGTs of users who connect to it, enabling impersonation to other services if the host is compromised. It does not disable Kerberos for LDAP binds, auto-promote service accounts to Domain Admin, or put BitLocker keys in SYSVOL.

en.question: What does the PrintNightmare class of vulnerabilities mainly abuse in a Windows environment?
options: It forges BGP communities on edge routers so every printer subnet is black-holed into Null0 before any spooler service can start at boot time
It replaces UEFI Secure Boot keys so only unsigned printer firmware can load before BitLocker unlocks the system volume on that host
It abuses the Windows Print Spooler so a remote or local attacker can run code as SYSTEM, often via malicious printer drivers
It converts every Domain Controller into a print server that stores NTDS.dit inside the shared printers$ folder for anonymous SMB reads
en.explanation: PrintNightmare-style issues abuse the Print Spooler (and related driver installation paths) to achieve remote/local code execution as SYSTEM. Mitigations include disabling the spooler where unused, restricting driver installation, and patching. It is not a BGP Null0 trick, Secure Boot key swap, or anonymous NTDS.dit share.

en.question: In Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) abuse, what does the ESC1 technique mainly rely on?
options: Stealing only the KRBTGT hash from a read-only Domain Controller backup tape so Silver Tickets can be forged with no certificate use at all afterward
A misconfigured certificate template that lets low-privilege users enroll and supply an arbitrary SAN to authenticate as another user
Forcing every workstation to trust a rogue DHCP option 252 WPAD entry so proxies intercept Kerberos AS-REQ messages on UDP port 88 only
Disabling SMB signing domain-wide through a single GPO so NTLM relay to LDAP becomes the only remaining prerequisite still called ESC1
en.explanation: ESC1 abuses overly permissive AD CS templates (e.g. client authentication EKU, enrollee-supplied SAN, Domain Users enrollment) so an attacker enrolls a certificate impersonating another principal and then uses it for authentication. It is not KRBTGT-only Silver Ticket theft, WPAD/DHCP 252 Kerberos interception, or SMB-signing GPO as the ESC1 core.

en.question: How does RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection) mainly differ from a traditional network or reverse-proxy WAF?
options: RASP only inspects BGP flowspec rules on the edge firewall appliance, while a WAF only validates OSPF LSAs before they enter Area 0 of the core
RASP replaces TLS entirely with cleartext HTTP inside the app container so the WAF can skip certificate pinning checks forever after every deploy
RASP runs exclusively as an offline malware sandbox that detonates uploaded binaries once, while a WAF must sit inline on every packet along the forwarding path
RASP instruments inside the running application to see real execution context, whereas a WAF typically filters HTTP at the edge without app internals
en.explanation: RASP hooks or instruments the application runtime (libraries, interpreters, agents) so detections use real code paths, data flows, and users—context a perimeter WAF usually lacks. A WAF still filters at HTTP/edge policy layer. RASP is not BGP/OSPF inspection, not a TLS-removal feature, and not merely an offline sandbox.

en.question: What is BloodHound mainly used for in Active Directory security assessments?
options: It replaces every Domain Controller’s KRBTGT password twice per hour so Golden Tickets expire before an attacker can forge any TGT at all
It acts as an inline WAF that blocks Kerberoasting TGS requests whenever an SPN belongs to a user account with a weak password hash
It encrypts LSASS memory with a hypervisor enclave so tools like Mimikatz can never read NTLM hashes or Kerberos tickets from RAM
It maps AD users, groups, computers, and ACLs as a graph to reveal attack paths such as paths to Domain Admin
en.explanation: BloodHound (and collectors like SharpHound) enumerate AD relationships and ACLs into a graph so analysts/attackers can find privilege-escalation paths (e.g. to Domain Admin). It does not rotate KRBTGT on a schedule, act as a WAF for Kerberoasting, or encrypt LSASS by itself.

en.question: In modern Active Directory abuse, what do Shadow Credentials mainly involve?
options: Writing a malicious service principal name on krbtgt so every TGS request is forced into unconstrained delegation toward a rogue host
Writing attacker-controlled keys into an account’s msDS-KeyCredentialLink so the attacker can authenticate as that principal via PKINIT
Disabling SMB signing and LDAP channel binding domain-wide with one GPO so NTLM relay to Certificate Services becomes the only step left
Replacing the domain’s DANE TLSA records so LDAPS clients accept a forged certificate chain from any public Web PKI intermediate CA
en.explanation: Shadow Credentials abuse the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute (often via Key Trust / Windows Hello for Business style keys) so an attacker who can write that attribute adds their key material and then obtains tickets as the victim using PKINIT. It is not krbtgt SPN unconstrained-delegation setup, a GPO that only disables signing/binding, or DANE TLSA replacement.

en.question: On a Microsoft Entra ID–joined Windows device, what is a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) mainly used for?
options: It is a one-time BitLocker recovery password escrowed only to Active Directory so offline disks can never unlock without a Domain Admin
It is a local SAM hash of the enrolled user’s password that Windows replays to NTLM services when Kerberos is unavailable on that subnet
It is a device-bound SSO refresh token that lets the user silently obtain access tokens for Entra ID–protected cloud apps and resources
It is an Azure Storage shared access signature that grants anonymous write to every blob container in the tenant until the next password change
en.explanation: A PRT is issued to Entra-joined/hybrid-joined devices and enables single sign-on: the device can obtain access tokens for cloud resources without prompting the user repeatedly. Theft/abuse of PRT material is a living-off-cloud style concern. It is not BitLocker escrow, a SAM/NTLM hash replay blob, or a tenant-wide anonymous SAS.

en.question: In cloud environments, why is SSRF that reaches the instance metadata service (IMDS, e.g. 169.254.169.254) especially dangerous?
options: It only lets an attacker change the VM hostname in DNS so TLS certificate pinning fails on the next reboot of every load balancer
It permanently disables the hypervisor firewall so every guest can send spoofed BGP updates into the provider backbone without IAM checks
It can expose temporary credentials or tokens that the instance role uses, letting the attacker call cloud APIs as that role
It forces the guest OS to downgrade all outbound TLS to SSLv3 so packet captures on the VPC mirror can decrypt every HTTPS session
en.explanation: IMDS often serves IAM role credentials (or similar short-lived tokens) to the instance. SSRF that can query that link-local endpoint can steal those credentials and abuse cloud APIs. It is not merely a hostname/DNS trick, a BGP spoof enabler, or an SSLv3 downgrade of all egress TLS.

en.question: What does an OAuth device-code phishing attack mainly trick a victim into doing?
options: Granting the attacker’s registered application consent by entering a short user code shown on a fake or attacker-controlled page
Installing a malicious browser extension that rewrites every Authorization header to a static Bearer token stolen from LSASS
Disabling MFA tenant-wide through a forged SAML assertion that the IdP accepts because the device code bypasses TLS entirely
Replacing the tenant’s JWKS endpoint with a rogue key so every previously issued refresh token validates forever without expiry
en.explanation: Device authorization flow shows a user code and a verification URI. Attackers phish victims into approving the attacker’s app (often via a convincing page), yielding tokens for the attacker. It is not an LSASS Bearer rewrite, an MFA-off SAML forge that skips TLS, or a permanent JWKS swap.

en.question: On Windows, what does abusing SeImpersonatePrivilege (e.g. Potato-family techniques) mainly achieve for a local attacker?
options: It rewrites the domain KRBTGT hash in AD so every TGT forged afterward is accepted as a Golden Ticket without needing DCSync rights
It disables Windows Defender Tamper Protection by swapping the ELAM driver signature database with an unsigned offline copy on disk
It forces every outbound SMB connection to fall back to NTLMv1 so a remote listener can capture crackable challenge-response pairs
It lets a service account (or similar) impersonate a more privileged token on the host, often escalating to SYSTEM locally
en.explanation: SeImpersonatePrivilege allows a process to impersonate clients that connect to it. Potato-style attacks coerce a privileged service to authenticate to the attacker’s pipe/listener and then impersonate that high-privilege token (often SYSTEM). It is not KRBTGT rewrite, ELAM/Tamper Protection bypass by itself, or a forced NTLMv1 downgrade of all SMB.

en.question: What does a PetitPotam-style attack mainly coerce a Windows host (often a DC) into doing?
options: Rewriting the domain KRBTGT hash on disk locally so every forged TGT validates afterward without needing any DCSync rights
Disabling Credential Guard by replacing the VBS launch policy with an unsigned offline registry hive copied from another host
Forcing every outbound SMB session down to NTLMv1 so a remote listener can capture and crack challenge-response pairs offline
Authenticating to an attacker-controlled listener (often via MS-EFSRPC), enabling NTLM relay or related follow-on abuse
en.explanation: PetitPotam abuses MS-EFSRPC (and similar) to coerce authentication toward an attacker. Combined with NTLM relay (or related techniques), that can lead to further domain compromise. It is not itself a KRBTGT rewrite, a Credential Guard bypass by hive swap, or a forced NTLMv1 downgrade of all SMB.

en.question: What did the Zerologon vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472) mainly allow an attacker on the network to do against an unpatched domain controller?
options: Read every BitLocker recovery key from Azure AD by spoofing only the Netlogon secure channel with an empty AES-GCM authentication tag
Disable Windows Defender Tamper Protection remotely by setting the Netlogon machine account password literally to the string zerologon
Spoof Netlogon secure-channel auth (all-zero IV flaw) and reset the DC machine account password to an empty or known value
Forge Kerberos Golden Tickets without ever touching KRBTGT, because Netlogon replaced PAC validation on every subsequent TGS-REQ
en.explanation: Zerologon abused a Netlogon crypto flaw (all-zero IV) so an attacker could impersonate a client and set the DC's machine account password to a known/empty value, enabling further takeover. It is not BitLocker key theft via empty GCM tags alone, a Defender Tamper Protection toggle, or Golden Tickets without KRBTGT.

en.question: What does enabling Windows Credential Guard mainly protect against on a supported host?
