en.question: What is the safe first step when a host shows signs of malware infection?
options: Keep using it normally in most production environments
Isolate it from the network and run a trusted scan
Share its files to coworkers
Disable all its logging across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: Isolating the host stops spread and C2, then a trusted scan and investigation can proceed before cleanup or reimaging.

en.question: What does a port scan accomplish for an attacker or auditor?
options: It patches vulnerable services in typical enterprise networks
It discovers which TCP/UDP ports and services are open on a host
It encrypts the target's disk in most production environments
It resets user passwords in typical enterprise networks across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: A port scan enumerates open ports and listening services, revealing the attack surface; it is reconnaissance, not a fix.

en.question: When monitoring security events, what should trigger escalation?
options: Every successful normal login during routine maintenance windows
A credible sign of a security incident beyond routine noise
A scheduled nightly backup finishing without additional tooling
A user changing their desktop wallpaper
en.explanation: Analysts escalate when evidence suggests a real incident (e.g. confirmed malware, data exfiltration), not for routine, benign events.

en.question: Which best describes asymmetric encryption?
options: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts
A public key encrypts and a matching private key decrypts
It never uses keys at all for day-to-day operations
It only works on data at rest in most production environments
en.explanation: Asymmetric (public-key) crypto uses a key pair: the public key encrypts (or verifies) and the private key decrypts (or signs).

en.question: Why is DHCP a security concern on an untrusted LAN?
options: It encrypts traffic too strongly when no other controls exist
A rogue DHCP server can hand out a malicious gateway or DNS
It uses TCP port 443 only in most production environments
It disables ARP entirely across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: A rogue DHCP server can assign a malicious default gateway/DNS to clients, enabling interception; DHCP snooping mitigates this.

en.question: Which example best fits 'something you are' as an authentication factor?
options: A PIN code
A fingerprint
A hardware token
A security question
en.explanation: Authentication factors are something you know (PIN), have (token) or are (biometric); a fingerprint is 'something you are'.

en.question: In the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis, which four core features are linked?
options: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim
Router, Switch, Firewall, Server
Red, Blue, Purple, Green during routine maintenance windows
Preparation, Detection, Recovery, Review
en.explanation: The Diamond Model links adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim to reason about an intrusion event.

en.question: Risk levels are often ranked as low, medium, high and extremely high mainly to help organizations do what?
options: Pick desk colors when no other controls exist
Prioritize which risks to treat first
Choose the office location
Set the Wi-Fi channel
en.explanation: Ranking risk severity lets organizations prioritize mitigation effort and budget on the most serious risks first.

en.question: What does asset management contribute to endpoint security?
options: It makes screens larger without additional tooling
It keeps an inventory so unknown or unpatched devices can be found
It encrypts email automatically according to common practice
It speeds up the CPU according to common practice in most production environments
en.explanation: A hardware/software inventory lets security teams spot unmanaged, rogue or unpatched devices that would otherwise be blind spots.

en.question: Which statement about spear phishing is correct?
options: It targets a specific person or organization with tailored content
It is always sent as a printed letter during routine maintenance windows
It never uses email without additional tooling
It only affects routers during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: Spear phishing is targeted: the attacker tailors the lure to a specific victim using personal or organizational details.

en.question: Which protocol secures web traffic by encrypting HTTP?
options: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS)
FTP across mixed vendor fleets
Telnet in most production environments
SNMPv1
en.explanation: HTTPS runs HTTP over TLS to encrypt web traffic; FTP, Telnet and SNMPv1 send data in cleartext by default.

en.question: When reviewing logs, which pattern most suggests a brute-force login attempt?
options: One successful login in the morning
Many failed logins for one account in a short time
A single DNS query according to common practice
A scheduled backup event when no other controls exist
en.explanation: A burst of failed authentications against an account (or many accounts) in a short window is a classic brute-force/spraying signature.

en.question: What is the main security role of a proxy server for outbound web access?
options: It assigns IP addresses to clients
It mediates and can filter/log web requests from clients
It replaces the firewall entirely in typical enterprise networks
It encrypts the local disk for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: A forward proxy mediates clients' outbound web requests, allowing filtering, logging and malware inspection of that traffic.

en.question: What does 'hardening' a system mean?
options: Adding more RAM to it for day-to-day operations during routine maintenance windows
Reducing its attack surface by removing unneeded services and tightening config
Painting the server case according to common practice
Increasing the monitor resolution according to common practice
en.explanation: Hardening reduces attack surface: disable unused services/ports, remove default accounts, apply secure settings and patches.

en.question: What is the main benefit of accounting (the third A in AAA)?
options: It blocks all network traffic for day-to-day operations
It records user actions for auditing and forensics
It encrypts the password database
It assigns VLANs automatically during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: Accounting logs what authenticated users did (commands, sessions, data), supporting auditing, billing and incident investigation.

en.question: What does a rootkit primarily try to do?
options: Improve system performance without additional tooling
Hide its presence and maintain privileged access on a system
Back up user files during routine maintenance windows
Update firmware safely when no other controls exist in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: A rootkit hides malware and maintains stealthy privileged access, often by subverting the OS so standard tools cannot see it.

en.question: Why are private IP ranges (like 10.0.0.0/8) not routable on the public internet?
options: They are reserved for internal use and dropped by internet routers
They are faster than public IPs across mixed vendor fleets
They are only for IPv6 for day-to-day operations without additional tooling
They are encrypted by design without additional tooling
en.explanation: RFC 1918 private ranges are reserved for internal networks and are not routed on the public internet, which is why NAT is used.

en.question: What are TTPs in threat analysis?
options: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures of an adversary
Transport Table Protocols
Trusted Terminal Ports during routine maintenance windows
Temporary Test Passwords according to common practice
en.explanation: TTPs describe how an adversary operates: their tactics (goals), techniques (methods) and procedures (specific implementations).

en.question: Why should incident documentation be updated and securely shared during a response?
options: To slow down the investigation without additional tooling
To keep responders coordinated and preserve an accurate record
To expose evidence publicly in typical enterprise networks
To delete all prior notes when no other controls exist according to common practice
en.explanation: Keeping documentation current and securely shared keeps the team coordinated and preserves an accurate, admissible record of the incident.

en.question: What do file and directory permissions primarily enforce?
options: Which users or processes may read
The screen refresh rate for day-to-day operations
The order of boot devices
The Wi-Fi channel width
en.explanation: Permissions enforce access control at the filesystem level, deciding which users/processes can read, write or execute each resource.

en.question: What does virtualization add to security planning in a data center?
options: It removes the need for any patching
Multiple isolated VMs share hardware
It makes all servers physical again
It disables logging by default without additional tooling
en.explanation: Virtualization consolidates many isolated VMs on shared hardware, so VM isolation, hypervisor hardening and snapshots become security concerns.

en.question: What is the core trait that makes social engineering effective?
options: It exploits human trust and behaviour rather than only technical flaws
It only works against old hardware according to common practice in typical enterprise networks
It requires physical access every time across mixed vendor fleets
It needs the victim's private key in most production environments
en.explanation: Social engineering manipulates people (trust, urgency, authority) to bypass technical controls, which is why awareness training matters.

en.question: What is the role of a Certificate Authority (CA) in PKI?
options: It stores user passwords when no other controls exist
It issues and vouches for the authenticity of digital certificates
It encrypts the hard disk in typical enterprise networks
It assigns IP addresses across mixed vendor fleets for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: A CA is a trusted third party that issues and signs certificates, vouching that a public key belongs to the named identity.

en.question: How do threat, vulnerability and exploit relate?
options: A threat is a weakness; an exploit is a natural disaster
A threat may use an exploit against a vulnerability to cause harm
They are three names for the same thing across mixed vendor fleets
An exploit always patches a vulnerability
en.explanation: A threat is a potential cause of harm; a vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is the method that uses that weakness.

en.question: In CVSS, what does the Attack Vector metric describe?
options: How far away the attacker can be to exploit the vulnerability
The cost of the exploit kit in typical enterprise networks
The colour of the alert in most production environments
The age of the patch without additional tooling in most production environments
en.explanation: Attack Vector rates whether the exploit needs physical, local, adjacent or network reach to the vulnerable component.

en.question: Which access control model assigns permissions based on the subject's job role?
options: DAC
MAC
RBAC
ABAC
en.explanation: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) grants rights according to roles; DAC is owner-driven, MAC is label-based, ABAC uses attributes.

en.question: What does Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) use to decide access?
options: Only a single shared password
Attributes of subject
The MAC address alone for day-to-day operations
The colour of the badge
en.explanation: ABAC evaluates attributes of the user, resource, action and context (time, location) against policies to allow or deny.

en.question: What is the core idea of defense in depth for a SOC analyst?
options: One perfect control is enough for day-to-day operations
Multiple overlapping controls raise the chance of detection and delay
Logging should be disabled to save space when no other controls exist
All traffic should be trusted inside the LAN
en.explanation: Defense in depth means layered controls so detection and delay remain possible even if one layer fails.

en.question: What five fields make up the classic 5-tuple used to isolate a host in network logs?
options: Source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol
Username, password, VLAN, SSID, gateway according to common practice
MAC, serial number, model, firmware, vendor
File hash, path, size, owner, ACL for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: The 5-tuple (src IP, dst IP, src port, dst port, protocol) uniquely identifies a flow and helps isolate a compromised host in grouped logs.

en.question: How does rule-based detection differ from behavioral detection?
options: Rule-based matches known signatures; behavioral looks for deviations from normal
Rule-based only works offline; behavioral only works online
They are identical approaches according to common practice without additional tooling
Behavioral never generates alerts when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Rule/signature detection matches known patterns; behavioral/statistical detection flags anomalies against a baseline of normal activity.

en.question: Why can encryption make security monitoring harder?
options: It slows down the CPU only in most production environments
Encrypted payloads hide content from network sensors that lack decryption
It deletes all logs in most production environments without additional tooling
It disables DHCP during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: End-to-end encryption hides payload content from NIDS/proxies that cannot decrypt, reducing visibility into malicious content.

en.question: How do attack surface and vulnerability differ?
options: Attack surface is the set of exposed points
They are synonyms during routine maintenance windows
Attack surface is always a bug
A vulnerability is the number of open ports only
en.explanation: Attack surface is the collection of entry points an adversary can try; a vulnerability is a concrete weakness that may exist on those points.

en.question: What type of data does NetFlow primarily provide for security monitoring?
options: Full packet payloads when no other controls exist
Session metadata such as who talked to whom
Disk encryption keys
Email body content across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: NetFlow (and similar flow data) records connection metadata — endpoints, ports, bytes, duration — without storing full payloads.

en.question: What does a full packet capture (PCAP) give you that NetFlow does not?
options: Only the source MAC address
The actual payload contents of the packets
Only the VLAN ID when no other controls exist
Only DHCP leases for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: PCAP stores complete packets including payloads, enabling deep content analysis that flow metadata alone cannot provide.

en.question: How does a next-generation firewall (NGFW) typically differ from a traditional stateful firewall?
options: An NGFW adds application awareness
An NGFW never tracks state
An NGFW only works on Layer 1
There is no difference in most production environments
en.explanation: NGFWs add application identification, URL/content filtering and often intrusion prevention and malware inspection on top of stateful filtering.

en.question: How can NAT/PAT reduce visibility for a SOC reviewing inbound traffic?
options: By hiding many internal hosts behind one public address
By deleting all NetFlow records across mixed vendor fleets
By encrypting the SIEM for day-to-day operations
By disabling DNS in most production environments
en.explanation: PAT multiplexes many internal hosts behind one public IP, so inbound logs may show only the public address unless internal logs are correlated.

en.question: Which best describes a protocol-based network attack?
options: Abusing protocol features or weaknesses (e.g. SYN floods
Only phishing via email in typical enterprise networks
Only physical theft of a laptop in most production environments
Only cracking offline password hashes
en.explanation: Protocol-based attacks misuse protocol behaviour (floods, amplification, malformed packets) to disrupt or deceive network services.

en.question: What is the main goal of a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack?
options: Inject malicious scripts into a trusted web page viewed by other users
Flood a DNS server with queries in typical enterprise networks
Steal a hardware security module for day-to-day operations
Rewrite BGP routes in most production environments in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: XSS injects attacker-controlled script into a page that victims' browsers trust, often to steal sessions or perform actions as the user.

en.question: What does a command injection attack against a web app typically try to do?
options: Run OS shell commands via unsanitized input
Improve the page layout for day-to-day operations
Rotate TLS certificates
Disable JavaScript in most production environments
en.explanation: Command injection passes attacker-controlled input into a shell or system call, letting the attacker run commands on the server.

en.question: How can generative AI change social-engineering attacks?
options: It can produce more convincing, personalized phishing at scale
It makes social engineering impossible in typical enterprise networks
It only helps defenders, never attackers
It removes the need for any network access
en.explanation: Generative AI can craft fluent, personalized phishing and deepfakes at scale, raising the quality of social-engineering lures.

en.question: What is the role of a command-and-control (C2) channel in an endpoint attack?
options: It lets the attacker remotely direct compromised hosts
It is the antivirus update feed
It is the DHCP lease renewal for day-to-day operations
It is the printer spooler across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: C2 is the communication path used by malware so the attacker can issue commands and receive data from compromised hosts.

en.question: Why do attackers use tunneling or encryption as evasion techniques?
options: To make malicious traffic look like or hide inside allowed protocols
To speed up legitimate downloads when no other controls exist
To reduce CPU use on the victim without additional tooling
To force patching in most production environments according to common practice
en.explanation: Tunneling and encryption hide C2 or exfiltration inside protocols that are allowed (HTTPS, DNS, SSH), bypassing simple filters.

en.question: How do certificates affect security monitoring of HTTPS traffic?
options: Without TLS interception or endpoint telemetry
Certificates delete all NetFlow
Certificates block ARP when no other controls exist
Certificates force IPv6 only
en.explanation: HTTPS encrypts payloads; without a TLS break-and-inspect point or host telemetry, network sensors see little of the content.

en.question: Which component of an X.509 certificate names the entity it belongs to?
options: The Subject field
The TTL of a DNS record
The VLAN ID
The MTU size
en.explanation: The Subject (and Subject Alternative Name) fields identify the entity the certificate was issued for.

en.question: What does a host-based intrusion detection system (HIDS) mainly monitor?
options: Activity and files on a single host
Only traffic between two routers
Only cloud billing in most production environments
Only printer queues
en.explanation: A HIDS watches host-level activity (logs, files, processes) on that machine, complementing network IDS.

en.question: In digital forensics, what is corroborative evidence?
options: Evidence that supports other evidence but is not sufficient alone
The only piece of evidence needed for day-to-day operations during routine maintenance windows
Evidence that contradicts the case for day-to-day operations
Evidence that must be deleted in most production environments
en.explanation: Corroborative evidence backs up other findings but would not prove the case by itself; best evidence is the most reliable primary source.

en.question: What does a malware sandbox (detonation chamber) report typically include?
options: Observed behaviour of the sample when executed in a controlled environment
The victim's salary across mixed vendor fleets when no other controls exist
The office floor plan during routine maintenance windows
The Wi-Fi password of the SOC during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: A sandbox runs a sample in isolation and reports behaviour (files, network, registry) to help analysts classify it safely.

en.question: In detection quality, what is a false positive?
options: An alert raised when there was no real threat
A correctly detected attack
A missed attack in typical enterprise networks
A successful login for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: A false positive is an alert that fires without a real malicious event, wasting analyst time; a false negative is a missed real attack.

en.question: How does deep packet inspection (DPI) differ from simple packet filtering?
options: DPI examines payload content beyond just headers and ports
DPI only looks at the Ethernet preamble
DPI disables all logging during routine maintenance windows
DPI only works on UDP in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: Packet filters use headers/ports; DPI inspects application-layer payload content to identify threats or applications.

en.question: What is a key difference between inline IPS and a passive tap for monitoring?
options: Inline can block traffic; a tap only observes a copy
A tap can block traffic; inline cannot
They are functionally identical
A tap encrypts all packets across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: An inline IPS sits in the path and can drop packets; a tap/SPAN only receives a copy and cannot block.

en.question: When analysing a PCAP of a suspected intrusion, which elements are key to identify first?
options: Source and destination addresses
Only the capture file name for day-to-day operations
Only the analyst's username
Only the screen brightness
en.explanation: Key intrusion elements in a PCAP are who talked to whom (IPs), on which ports, which protocols, and what payloads look like.

en.question: Which artifact is commonly used to identify known malware samples across systems?
options: A cryptographic file hash (e.g. SHA-256)
The colour of the desktop background
The printer model in most production environments
The office zip code
en.explanation: File hashes uniquely fingerprint samples so the same malware can be recognized across hosts and threat intel feeds.

en.question: Why do SOC analysts learn basic regular expressions?
options: To match and extract patterns in logs and packet data efficiently
To replace the need for firewalls when no other controls exist
To assign IP addresses in most production environments
To configure RAID in most production environments according to common practice
en.explanation: Regex lets analysts quickly filter and extract patterns (IPs, URLs, hashes) from large log and PCAP datasets.

en.question: What does vulnerability management mainly involve?
options: Identifying, prioritizing and remediating weaknesses over time
Only buying new firewalls during routine maintenance windows
Only resetting passwords monthly without additional tooling
Only painting server racks according to common practice when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Vulnerability management is the ongoing process of finding, ranking and fixing weaknesses across the estate.

en.question: According to NIST SP 800-61, which activity belongs to the Preparation phase?
options: Building playbooks, contacts and tooling before an incident
Deleting all evidence after an incident
Ignoring alerts in most production environments
Sharing passwords on a whiteboard for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Preparation covers policies, playbooks, contacts, tooling and training so the team can respond effectively when an incident occurs.

en.question: According to the order of volatility, which evidence should be captured before a disk image?
options: CPU registers and RAM contents
Archived tape backups from last year
Printed manuals
Wall posters when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Volatile data (CPU, RAM, network state) disappears on power-off, so it is collected before less volatile storage such as disk images.

en.question: Which element is used when profiling a network for anomaly detection?
options: Typical throughput, session duration, ports and critical asset address space
The colour of the patch cables in typical enterprise networks
The brand of the chairs for day-to-day operations in most production environments
The font used in emails in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: Network profiling baselines throughput, session lengths, ports in use and critical ranges so deviations stand out.

en.question: When profiling a server for security, which item is useful to baseline?
options: Listening ports, logged-in users, running processes and applications
The wallpaper image during routine maintenance windows
The keyboard language only when no other controls exist
The desk height according to common practice when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Server profiling notes listening ports, accounts, processes and apps so unexpected services or users become visible.

en.question: Which data type is protected health information (PHI)?
options: Medical records identifying a patient
A public weather forecast
An open-source software license
A network cable length in most production environments
en.explanation: PHI is health information that can identify an individual and is protected under frameworks such as HIPAA.

en.question: What do SOC metrics such as time-to-detect and time-to-contain measure?
options: How quickly the team finds and limits an incident
How fast printers print during routine maintenance windows
How bright the SOC lights are in typical enterprise networks
How many coffee cups are used
en.explanation: SOC metrics like TTD/TTC/TTR quantify response speed so the organisation can improve detection and containment.

en.question: In a suspicious DNS query seen in a PCAP, which fields are most useful to inspect?
options: Query name, query type and response addresses
Only the Ethernet FCS during routine maintenance windows
Only the IP TTL according to common practice
Only the TCP window size
en.explanation: DNS analysis focuses on the queried name, type (A/AAAA/TXT/MX) and the answers returned, which often reveal C2 or tunneling.

en.question: What does a buffer overflow endpoint attack mainly try to achieve?
options: Overwrite memory to alter program control flow
Improve memory safety during routine maintenance windows
Compress the binary in typical enterprise networks
Update the BIOS securely
en.explanation: A buffer overflow writes past a buffer's bounds to corrupt memory and often hijack control flow for arbitrary code execution.

en.question: What is threat hunting?
options: Proactively searching for threats that automated detections may have missed
Waiting for vendors to email indicators according to common practice
Deleting all logs weekly during routine maintenance windows
Disabling EDR to reduce noise when no other controls exist in most production environments
en.explanation: Threat hunting is a proactive, hypothesis-driven search for adversary activity that existing alerts may not have caught.

en.question: What does DevSecOps emphasize?
options: Integrating security into the CI/CD pipeline instead of treating it as a final gate
Removing all automated tests without additional tooling in typical enterprise networks
Shipping without any reviews in most production environments
Storing secrets in source code in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: DevSecOps builds security into development and delivery pipelines (scanning, policy as code) rather than bolting it on at the end.

en.question: An analyst sees a Windows Security log with many 4625 failures followed by a 4624 for the same account from an unusual IP. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: Possible brute-force that eventually succeeded
A successful disk defragmentation
A normal DHCP renew across mixed vendor fleets
A printer firmware update
en.explanation: Repeated logon failures (4625) then a success (4624) from an odd source is a classic sign of a successful brute-force or spraying attack.

en.question: What characterizes a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack?
options: Many coordinated sources overwhelm a target's capacity
A single user mistypes a password once
A scheduled antivirus scan
A firmware update window in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: DDoS uses many (often botnet) sources to flood a target beyond its capacity, making service unavailable.

en.question: What kind of data does Application Visibility and Control (AVC) typically add?
options: Identification of applications beyond just port numbers
Only Layer-1 signal strength when no other controls exist
Only the serial numbers of switches
Only the office temperature in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: AVC classifies traffic by application (not just port), enabling policies and monitoring based on what apps are actually in use.

en.question: An alert shows a proxy log for a rare domain, an IPS signature hit on the same flow, and NetFlow with a large outbound byte count. What should the analyst do first?
options: Correlate the sources to confirm a real exfiltration or C2 case
Ignore all three because they conflict for day-to-day operations
Delete the NetFlow in typical enterprise networks
Disable the proxy according to common practice
en.explanation: Multiple independent sensors agreeing on the same flow raises confidence; correlate timestamps, IPs and users before containment.

en.question: Which cloud-specific threat involves stealing API keys that grant broad access to cloud resources?
options: Compromised credentials and insecure APIs
Cable cut at the ISP for day-to-day operations
Printer paper jam according to common practice
Monitor backlight failure
en.explanation: Cloud breaches often stem from leaked API keys or weak APIs that grant wide access to storage and compute resources.

en.question: What is a prompt injection attack against an AI/LLM system?
options: Crafting input that overrides the model's instructions to make it leak data or act wrongly
Injecting SQL into a database via a form during routine maintenance windows
Flooding a VPN concentrator in most production environments in typical enterprise networks
Overwriting BIOS firmware for day-to-day operations in most production environments
en.explanation: Prompt injection crafts user input that hijacks or overrides the system prompt, causing data leakage or unintended actions.

en.question: What does 'system prompt leakage' risk in an LLM deployment?
options: Exposing hidden instructions that reveal policies or secrets to the user
Losing the GPU driver across mixed vendor fleets in most production environments
Breaking DHCP leases during routine maintenance windows
Disabling syslog for day-to-day operations without additional tooling
en.explanation: If an LLM reveals its hidden system prompt, attackers learn policies, tool instructions or secrets embedded there.

en.question: Why is post-quantum cryptography (PQC) becoming relevant for security architects?
options: Large quantum computers may break widely used public-key algorithms
PQC makes Wi-Fi faster across mixed vendor fleets during routine maintenance windows
PQC replaces Ethernet cables in most production environments
PQC removes the need for MFA without additional tooling
en.explanation: PQC algorithms are designed to resist attacks from large-scale quantum computers that could break RSA and ECC.

en.question: What is MASQUE in modern encrypted transport?
options: A set of HTTP/3 mechanisms to proxy traffic over QUIC
A Layer-2 spanning-tree variant
A Windows event ID according to common practice
A RADIUS attribute for VLANs without additional tooling
en.explanation: MASQUE (Multiplexed Application Substrate over QUIC Encryption) defines HTTP/3 proxying so traffic can be securely relayed over QUIC.

en.question: Which Cisco VPN technology builds hub-and-spoke or spoke-to-spoke IPsec overlays with NHRP?
options: DMVPN
GETVPN
SSL clientless portal only
L2TP without IPsec
en.explanation: DMVPN uses mGRE and NHRP to build scalable hub-and-spoke (and spoke-to-spoke) IPsec VPN overlays.

en.question: What does GETVPN mainly provide in an enterprise WAN?
options: Group-encrypted traffic over a private WAN without per-peer tunnels
Guest Wi-Fi captive portal for day-to-day operations
Email spam filtering when no other controls exist in typical enterprise networks
Endpoint disk encryption across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: GETVPN uses GDOI group keys so sites on a private WAN encrypt traffic without building individual peer tunnels.

en.question: What is the core principle of a zero trust architecture?
options: Never trust, always verify
Trust all traffic inside the corporate LAN
Disable logging to reduce cost when no other controls exist
Open all ports for easier support
en.explanation: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust based on network location; every access request is authenticated, authorized and continuously evaluated.

en.question: What is Cisco SAFE in security architecture discussions?
options: A design guide for secure architectures across places in the network
A cable colour standard in most production environments
A DHCP option number for day-to-day operations without additional tooling
A BGP community value for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Cisco SAFE provides design guidance and business flows for building secure architectures across campus, WAN, data center and cloud.

en.question: When choosing between IPS and firewall capabilities, what does an IPS mainly add?
options: Deep inspection to detect and block exploit/malware patterns in allowed traffic
Only Layer-2 MAC filtering across mixed vendor fleets
Only DHCP address assignment for day-to-day operations
Only cable testing according to common practice in most production environments
en.explanation: Firewalls enforce allow/deny policy; IPS inspects permitted traffic for exploit and malware patterns and can block them.

en.question: Which Layer-2 control helps stop rogue DHCP servers on a Cisco switch?
options: DHCP snooping
STP PortFast only
LLDP
CDP across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: DHCP snooping builds a trusted binding table and drops DHCP replies from untrusted ports, blocking rogue DHCP servers.

en.question: What does Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) use to validate ARP packets?
options: The DHCP snooping binding database
The BGP routing table
The NTP stratum without additional tooling
The SNMP community string
en.explanation: DAI checks ARP against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops ARP packets that do not match trusted bindings.

en.question: Why do security teams use CIS Benchmarks for devices such as Secure Firewall (FTD) and IOS XE?
options: They provide consensus hardening recommendations
They replace the need for any authentication
They define Wi-Fi channel plans only
They set the office thermostat according to common practice
en.explanation: CIS Benchmarks offer vendor-agnostic, consensus hardening baselines that reduce common misconfigurations on network and security devices.

en.question: When troubleshooting AAA, how do TACACS+ and RADIUS mainly differ for device administration?
options: TACACS+ separates auth/author/acct and encrypts the full payload
RADIUS always uses TCP 49; TACACS+ uses UDP 1812 in typical enterprise networks
They are identical in every way when no other controls exist
TACACS+ cannot authorize commands without additional tooling
en.explanation: TACACS+ (TCP) encrypts the whole packet and separates AAA functions, making it preferred for device admin; RADIUS mainly encrypts the password field.

en.question: Which protocol should replace SNMPv1/v2c for secure device management?
options: SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy
Telnet for day-to-day operations
HTTP without TLS according to common practice
TFTP without additional tooling
en.explanation: SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption (authPriv), unlike cleartext communities in SNMPv1/v2c.

en.question: On Cisco Secure Firewall (FTD), what do Access Control Policy rules with AVC and URL filtering enable?
options: Allow/block based on application and URL category
Only MAC address filtering
Only static NAT without additional tooling
Only OSPF route filtering for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: FTD Access Control can match applications (AVC) and URL categories, enabling intent-based allow/block beyond 5-tuples.

en.question: Which client is commonly used with Cisco Secure Firewall for remote-access VPN?
options: Cisco Secure Client (formerly AnyConnect)
Only a TFTP client for day-to-day operations
Only HyperTerminal according to common practice
Only a DHCP client
en.explanation: Cisco Secure Client (AnyConnect) provides remote-access VPN (and other modules) to Secure Firewall / ASA headends.

en.question: When an IPsec VPN tunnel on FTD fails to establish, which step is most useful first?
options: Verify proposals, identities, routing and debug/log messages for Phase 1/2 failures
Replace all Ethernet cables immediately in most production environments
Disable logging without additional tooling across mixed vendor fleets when no other controls exist
Change the office SSID without additional tooling in most production environments
en.explanation: Tunnel bring-up failures are usually IKE proposal mismatch, identity/PSK/cert issues or routing; check logs/debugs for Phase 1 vs Phase 2.

en.question: In the Cloud Shared Responsibility Model for IaaS, who typically hardens the guest OS?
options: The customer
Only the cloud provider
Nobody without additional tooling
The ISP
en.explanation: In IaaS the provider secures the hypervisor and facility; the customer is responsible for the guest OS, apps and data.

en.question: What is Cisco Secure Workload (formerly Tetration) mainly used for?
options: Workload microsegmentation and visibility based on observed application flows
Guest Wi-Fi splash pages according to common practice
Cable certification without additional tooling during routine maintenance windows
Email signatures according to common practice when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Secure Workload maps application dependencies and enforces microsegmentation policies on workloads across data center and cloud.

en.question: Why might a SCOR-level design send cloud security logs into Splunk?
options: To centralize monitoring and correlation across cloud and on-prem sources
To delete cloud logs automatically for day-to-day operations
To replace IAM in typical enterprise networks according to common practice
To assign private IPs for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: Ingesting cloud logs into Splunk (or similar SIEM) enables unified detection and investigation across hybrid estates.

en.question: What is eBPF commonly used for in modern workload security?
options: Safe, programmable kernel-level observability and policy without loading classic modules
Replacing TLS certificates across mixed vendor fleets during routine maintenance windows
Assigning VLANs on access switches according to common practice
Drawing network diagrams in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: eBPF runs sandboxed programs in the kernel for high-performance observability and security policy on modern Linux workloads.

en.question: What does Infrastructure as Code (IaC) security focus on in DevSecOps?
options: Scanning templates and pipelines for misconfigurations before deployment
Painting server racks in typical enterprise networks
Choosing desk chairs according to common practice across mixed vendor fleets
Setting monitor brightness without additional tooling
en.explanation: IaC security scans Terraform/CloudFormation/etc. and CI pipelines for insecure defaults before infrastructure is deployed.

en.question: How does Security Service Edge (SSE) differ from the broader SASE concept?
options: SSE is the security services (SWG, CASB, ZTNA)
SSE is only a firewall; SASE is only Wi-Fi
They are identical marketing terms with no technical difference
SSE replaces Ethernet entirely in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: SSE covers cloud-delivered security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS); SASE combines those with WAN networking (typically SD-WAN).

en.question: What does Cisco Secure Access Secure Internet Access primarily protect?
options: Users' access to the public internet with cloud-delivered security controls
Only east-west traffic inside a single rack in most production environments
Only serial console ports in most production environments
Only undersea cables across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: Secure Internet Access applies SWG/CASB-style controls to users browsing the public internet via Cisco Secure Access.

en.question: What is Secure Private Access (SPA) in Cisco Secure Access mainly about?
options: Zero-trust access to private applications without exposing the whole network
Opening every port on the firewall during routine maintenance windows
Disabling MFA for day-to-day operations according to common practice
Bridging all VLANs together across mixed vendor fleets in most production environments
en.explanation: SPA provides ZTNA-style access to specific private apps, reducing the need to put users on the full corporate network.

en.question: Why configure DLP and AI guardrails on Secure Internet Access?
options: To stop sensitive data leaving and constrain risky AI tool usage
To increase download speed according to common practice
To assign IP addresses according to common practice
To reboot access points nightly during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: DLP prevents sensitive data exfiltration via web/SaaS; AI guardrails limit risky prompts or destinations for generative AI tools.

en.question: What do Cisco Secure Access Investigate scores help an analyst understand?
options: How risky a destination or domain appears based on threat intelligence
The physical temperature of a router across mixed vendor fleets
The length of a patch cable according to common practice
The brightness of a LED in typical enterprise networks during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: Investigate scores summarize threat intel risk for domains/destinations so analysts can prioritize blocks and investigations.

en.question: How do EPP and EDR mainly differ?
options: EPP focuses on prevention
EPP only encrypts disks; EDR only prints logs
They are the same acronym in most production environments
EDR replaces the need for any network firewall
en.explanation: Endpoint Protection Platforms emphasize prevention (AV/AV); EDR adds telemetry, detection, investigation and response capabilities.

en.question: What is endpoint posture assessment used for before granting network access?
options: Checking whether the device meets security requirements (patches
Measuring the user's typing speed in most production environments
Counting open browser tabs in typical enterprise networks
Choosing a desktop wallpaper when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Posture assessment verifies device health (updates, encryption, AV status) and can quarantine non-compliant devices.

en.question: What is Cisco Secure Malware Analytics (Threat Grid) mainly used for?
options: Sandbox detonation and malware analysis with threat intelligence
Assigning OSPF process IDs across mixed vendor fleets
Drawing floor plans in most production environments without additional tooling
Configuring PoE budgets when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Secure Malware Analytics detonates and analyses samples in a sandbox and enriches results with threat intelligence.

en.question: When configuring Cisco Secure Endpoint, what is a primary goal?
options: Deploy the connector and policies to prevent and detect malware on hosts
Replace the core switch in most production environments
Disable all USB ports forever without policy in typical enterprise networks
Turn off cloud analytics always in most production environments
en.explanation: Secure Endpoint deploys connectors and policies for prevention, detection and response against malware on endpoints.

en.question: An analyst reviews a Cisco Secure Endpoint malware detection event. What should they examine first?
options: File hash, path, process lineage and disposition to decide isolation or allow
Only the laptop colour in most production environments without additional tooling
Only the user's favourite font across mixed vendor fleets
Only the DHCP lease time during routine maintenance windows
en.explanation: Detection events include hash, path, parent process and disposition; those guide whether to isolate, remediate or tune a false positive.

en.question: What does Cisco Security Email Threat Defense mainly protect against?
options: Malicious and phishing email threats with detection and remediation
Layer-2 loops without additional tooling
PoE overload for day-to-day operations during routine maintenance windows
DNS TTL mismatches across mixed vendor fleets
en.explanation: Email Threat Defense focuses on detecting and remediating phishing and malware delivered by email.

en.question: In Cisco ISE, what does profiling mainly help with?
options: Identifying device types so policy can treat printers
Increasing Wi-Fi transmit power for day-to-day operations
Compressing NetFlow across mixed vendor fleets
Choosing rack colours in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: ISE profiling classifies endpoints (printer, IP phone, PC) from network probes so authorization policies can be device-aware.

en.question: What does device compliance checking typically verify before full network access?
options: Whether the endpoint meets security posture requirements
Whether the user likes the wallpaper
Whether the desk is adjustable according to common practice
Whether the mouse is wireless without additional tooling
en.explanation: Compliance/posture checks confirm patches, disk encryption, AV and similar controls before granting full access.

en.question: What does MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass) provide when 802.1X is not possible?
options: Fallback authentication using the device MAC address
Full mutual certificate authentication
Encrypted DNS only without additional tooling
Automatic BGP peering in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: MAB authenticates endpoints that cannot do 802.1X (printers, some IoT) by their MAC address, usually with limited access.

en.question: What is Change of Authorization (CoA) used for with ISE?
options: Dynamically changing a session's authorization (e.g. quarantine) without waiting for re-login
Changing the device hostname overnight across mixed vendor fleets during routine maintenance windows
Rotating rack PDU phases for day-to-day operations across mixed vendor fleets
Updating the wall colour during routine maintenance windows for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: CoA lets ISE push a new authorization state mid-session, such as quarantining a non-compliant host.

en.question: Which technique tunnels data inside DNS queries to bypass typical firewalls?
options: DNS tunneling
STP root guard
Port security sticky MAC
LLDP-MED
en.explanation: DNS tunneling encodes data in DNS queries/responses, often allowed through firewalls, for C2 or exfiltration.

en.question: What do Cisco XDR and Splunk-style SIEM/SOAR platforms mainly provide together?
options: Cross-domain detection
Only cable management
Only PoE budgeting in most production environments
Only Wi-Fi channel planning
en.explanation: XDR correlates multi-domain telemetry; SIEM/SOAR platforms like Splunk add search, detection content and automated response.

en.question: In a zero-trust design, what does Cisco Duo Device Trust mainly verify?
options: That the authenticating device is a managed
That the Ethernet cable is Cat6
That the monitor supports 4K without additional tooling
That the chair has lumbar support
en.explanation: Duo Device Trust checks device health/management state as part of adaptive access decisions in a zero-trust architecture.

en.question: What does Duo Trust Monitor help security teams notice?
options: Unusual authentication patterns that may indicate account takeover
The temperature of the UPS during routine maintenance windows
The length of fiber runs in typical enterprise networks in most production environments
The number of patch panels in typical enterprise networks
en.explanation: Trust Monitor highlights anomalous authentications (new location, impossible travel, new device) that may signal account compromise.

en.question: How does Splunk help manage and automate security events in a SCOR-aligned SOC?
options: Search, correlate and trigger response actions on security data at scale
Replace all firewalls with search queries for day-to-day operations
Assign OSPF areas across mixed vendor fleets for day-to-day operations
Configure EtherChannel only during routine maintenance windows without additional tooling
en.explanation: Splunk ingests and searches security data at scale and, with SOAR/automation, can trigger response actions from detections.

en.question: Which OWASP-related issue involves tricking a user's browser into making unwanted authenticated requests?
options: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
SQL injection only
ARP spoofing during routine maintenance windows
STP attack without additional tooling
en.explanation: CSRF abuses the browser's authenticated session to make the victim's browser send unintended state-changing requests.

en.question: Which control best reduces successful phishing clicks?
options: User awareness training plus MFA and email threat defense
Disabling all email during routine maintenance windows
Removing DNS across mixed vendor fleets according to common practice
Turning off all logging without additional tooling
en.explanation: Layered anti-phishing controls combine awareness training, MFA (limits credential reuse impact) and email security filtering.

en.question: What does security intelligence sharing mainly enable between organisations?
options: Faster recognition of known bad indicators across peers
Slower patch cycles during routine maintenance windows
Open admin shares during routine maintenance windows
Disabled TLS in most production environments according to common practice
en.explanation: Sharing threat intelligence (IoCs, TTPs) lets peers block and detect known bad activity faster than working in isolation.

en.question: What does Duo Adaptive Access mainly adjust based on risk signals?
options: Authentication requirements such as step-up MFA or block
The STP root priority in typical enterprise networks
The OSPF hello timer during routine maintenance windows
The PoE power class without additional tooling in most production environments
en.explanation: Adaptive Access policies raise or lower authentication strength (or deny) based on risk signals like new device or unusual location.

en.question: What is Cisco Security Cloud Control used for in managing security devices?
options: Centralised cloud management of multiple security devices and policies
Only drawing rack diagrams across mixed vendor fleets when no other controls exist
Only selling cables during routine maintenance windows
Only configuring analog modems when no other controls exist
en.explanation: Security Cloud Control (formerly CDO) provides centralised cloud-based management across multiple Cisco security devices.

en.question: Why is HTTPS a common exfiltration channel?
options: It is widely allowed and its encrypted payload hides content from simple inspection
It is always blocked by default when no other controls exist
It cannot carry files when no other controls exist according to common practice
It only works on printers in most production environments for day-to-day operations
en.explanation: HTTPS is usually permitted outbound and encryption conceals what is being transferred unless TLS inspection or endpoint DLP is in place.

en.question: Sysmon on a workstation logs event ID 13: a new value 'Updater' under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run pointing to C:\Users\ana\AppData\Roaming\upd.exe, which is unsigned. What does this most likely show?
options: Persistence: the program will start each time the user signs in, a common trick for malware placed in AppData
A normal Windows Update task, since Windows Update always keeps its updater in each user's AppData Roaming folder
Privilege escalation to SYSTEM, because writing to the Run key gives the program full admin rights at the next boot
A failed install that Windows rolled back, since Sysmon event 13 only appears when a registry change is reverted
en.explanation: Sysmon event 13 records a registry value being set. The HKCU Run key launches its entries at user logon, so an unsigned exe in AppData added there is classic persistence (MITRE T1547.001). Windows Update doesn't live in AppData, an HKCU Run entry runs with the user's rights, not SYSTEM, and event 13 logs a change being made, not reverted.

en.question: A file server logs event 4624 with logon type 10 for the account 'backup_svc' at 03:12, from a public IP abroad. That account is normally used only by a scheduled job on the backup server. What does this most likely mean?
options: The scheduled backup job ran early, because type 10 is the logon type Windows uses for every scheduled task it runs
A user unlocked a locked screen on the console, since type 10 marks a workstation unlock done with cached details
Someone signed in interactively over RDP with the service account, likely stolen, from an external address
A network share was opened by a backup client, since type 10 is used for SMB access to shared folders on servers
en.explanation: Logon type 10 is RemoteInteractive, meaning Remote Desktop. A service account that should only log on as a batch job (type 4) or over the network (type 3) now has an RDP session from a foreign public IP at night, a strong sign of stolen credentials and exposed RDP. Unlocks are type 7, scheduled tasks are type 4 and SMB share access is type 3.

en.question: DNS logs show one laptop sending thousands of TXT queries per hour to random-looking subdomains of a single new domain, such as 'a9f3k2...q7.cdn-sync.xyz', each label near 60 characters. What is the most likely activity?
options: A content delivery network balancing load, since CDNs always use long random subdomains with TXT records for each file
A broken DNS cache on the laptop, which keeps asking again because every answer it gets expires right after it arrives
SPF and DKIM checks by the mail client, because email apps look up TXT records for each message they are sending
DNS tunnelling for C2 or data theft, with data encoded in the subdomain labels and replies carried in TXT records
en.explanation: Long, high-entropy labels under one rare domain, lots of TXT queries and a single host are the signs of DNS tunnelling (tools like iodine or dnscat2). Data rides out in the query names and commands come back in TXT answers, slipping past firewalls that allow DNS. CDNs use normal A/AAAA lookups, a bad cache doesn't make random names and mail clients don't do SPF/DKIM lookups for outgoing mail.

pt.question: Numa rede de controlo industrial, que objetivo de segurança costuma ter prioridade sobre os outros?
options: Compressão dos dados do historian
Confidencialidade de todos os fluxos e ficheiros
Anonimato dos operadores
Disponibilidade do processo e segurança física
pt.explanation: Nas redes OT a ordem habitual é Disponibilidade, depois Integridade e só depois Confidencialidade (AIC), porque parar o processo custa dinheiro ou pode causar danos.

pt.question: Porque é que os sistemas OT são atualizados muito menos vezes do que os PCs de escritório?
options: Os patches exigem validação do fabricante e paragem
Nunca se ligam a nenhuma rede, por isso os patches são inúteis
Os sistemas operativos em OT não se atualizam
O antivírus já substitui todos os patches
pt.explanation: Os patches em OT costumam ser certificados pelo fabricante de automação e aplicados em paragens planeadas, porque uma alteração não testada pode parar a produção.

pt.question: No modelo Purdue, em que nível costumam estar os PLC que executam a lógica de controlo?
options: Nível 1
Nível 3
Nível 0
Nível 4
pt.explanation: O nível 0 tem sensores e atuadores, o nível 1 os controladores básicos (PLC, DCS), o nível 2 as HMI/SCADA de supervisão e o nível 3 as operações do site.

pt.question: Que sistemas pertencem ao nível 4 do modelo Purdue?
options: Sensores de campo e variadores
HMI de operador na linha
ERP, email e planeamento do negócio
Relés de segurança e barreiras óticas da máquina
pt.explanation: O nível 4 é planeamento e logística do negócio (email, acesso ao ERP, relatórios) e é tratado como extensão da rede empresarial.

pt.question: Qual é a regra principal para o tráfego que atravessa uma DMZ industrial (nível 3.5)?
options: Só o ICMP é bloqueado entre as zonas
Qualquer tráfego pode passar direto se estiver cifrado com HTTPS
Nenhuma sessão passa direta; os dados são intermediados
PCs empresariais podem chegar diretamente aos PLC na porta TCP 502
pt.explanation: Numa IDMZ nenhum fluxo vai diretamente da zona empresarial para a industrial: as sessões terminam em brokers, jump hosts ou servidores espelhados (por exemplo um historian replicado).

pt.question: Os analistas do negócio precisam de dados de produção do historian da fábrica. Qual é o desenho habitual com IDMZ?
options: Abrir uma regra de firewall do escritório diretamente para os PLC
Pôr os PCs dos analistas na zona de célula/área
Espelhar o historian na IDMZ para eles consultarem
Fazer bridge da VLAN do escritório para a de controlo
pt.explanation: Um historian replicado ou espelhado na IDMZ permite aos utilizadores empresariais ler dados sem qualquer sessão direta para os níveis 0 a 3.

pt.question: Que porta TCP usa o Modbus TCP por omissão?
pt.explanation: O Modbus TCP escuta na porta TCP 502. A 102 é ISO-TSAP (S7comm, MMS do IEC 61850), a 44818 é a mensagem explícita EtherNet/IP e a 20000 é DNP3.

pt.question: Que afirmação sobre a segurança do Modbus está correta?
options: Cada trama Modbus TCP é assinada com certificado por omissão
O Modbus RTU cifra os dados com AES-128
O Modbus pede uma password ao cliente antes de cada escrita
O Modbus clássico não tem autenticação nem cifra
pt.explanation: O Modbus RTU/TCP clássico envia comandos em claro e sem autenticação, por isso qualquer host que chegue ao equipamento pode ler ou escrever. O Modbus/TCP Security junta TLS numa porta separada.

pt.question: Um cliente Modbus tem de ler um setpoint de 16 bits que também pode alterar. Em que tipo de dado está?
options: Coil
Input register
Discrete input
Holding register
pt.explanation: Os holding registers são valores de 16 bits de leitura/escrita. Os input registers são de 16 bits só de leitura, as coils de 1 bit leitura/escrita e as discrete inputs de 1 bit só de leitura.

pt.question: Que código de função Modbus lê holding registers?
pt.explanation: A função 03 lê holding registers. A 01 lê coils, a 05 escreve uma coil e a 16 (0x10) escreve vários registos.

pt.question: Num barramento Modbus RTU em RS-485, o que identifica o equipamento que deve responder a um pedido?
options: O seu endereço MAC transportado no cabeçalho da trama
O seu endereço IP e a porta 502
O endereço de escravo (unidade) no primeiro byte
A tag de VLAN adicionada pela gateway
pt.explanation: As tramas Modbus RTU começam pelo endereço de escravo (1 a 247), seguido do código de função, dos dados e de um CRC-16. No barramento série não há MAC nem IP.

pt.question: Uma gateway Modbus TCP-RTU tem timeouts só nos equipamentos no fim de um troço RS-485 comprido. O que deve verificar primeiro?
options: O servidor DNS configurado na gateway Modbus
A terminação e a polarização nas pontas
O custo OSPF configurado no uplink da gateway
O certificado TLS instalado no PLC do fim da linha
pt.explanation: Troços RS-485 compridos precisam de terminação de 120 Ω nas duas pontas e polarização correta; sem terminação há reflexões que corrompem as tramas dos nós distantes.

pt.question: No EtherNet/IP, como são normalmente transportados os dados de I/O cíclicos (mensagens implícitas)?
options: TCP porta 44818 dentro de uma sessão TLS
TCP porta 502 com um CRC no fim
UDP porta 2222, muitas vezes em multicast
Tramas Layer 2 puras com Ethertype 0x8892
pt.explanation: As mensagens implícitas (Classe 1) de I/O do EtherNet/IP usam UDP 2222, em unicast ou multicast. As explícitas usam TCP 44818. O Ethertype 0x8892 é do PROFINET RT.

pt.question: O que define o RPI (Requested Packet Interval) numa ligação de I/O EtherNet/IP?
options: O tamanho máximo da trama Ethernet
O número de sessões CIP que o adaptador permite
O temporizador de retransmissão TCP
A frequência com que o produtor envia os dados
pt.explanation: O RPI é a cadência acordada de uma ligação de I/O CIP, por exemplo de 10 em 10 ms. Um RPI mais pequeno significa mais pacotes por segundo na rede.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre mensagens CIP explícitas e implícitas?
options: As explícitas são vídeo multicast; as implícitas voz
As explícitas usam UDP; as implícitas usam sempre TCP
As explícitas exigem PROFINET; as implícitas exigem Modbus RTU
As explícitas são pedido/resposta; as implícitas I/O cíclico
pt.explanation: As mensagens explícitas são transações pedido/resposta a pedido (configuração, diagnóstico) sobre TCP. As implícitas transportam I/O em tempo real de forma cíclica sobre UDP.

pt.question: O modelo produtor/consumidor do CIP significa que:
options: Cada consumidor interroga o produtor à vez
Só um consumidor pode ler cada tag
Um produtor envia dados que muitos equipamentos consomem
Cada consumidor tem de confirmar todos os pacotes que recebe
pt.explanation: Com produtor/consumidor, um equipamento produz os dados uma vez (por exemplo em multicast) e qualquer número de consumidores os usa, em vez de cada um interrogar separadamente.

pt.question: O I/O multicast EtherNet/IP inunda todas as portas de uma célula Layer 2 plana e torna lentos os variadores antigos. Qual é a correção padrão?
options: IGMP snooping com um IGMP querier ativo na VLAN
Desligar o spanning tree em todos os switches IE
Subir o MTU para 9000 bytes em todo o lado
Ativar port security com um MAC por porta
pt.explanation: O IGMP snooping limita o multicast às portas que aderiram ao grupo, mas numa célula só Layer 2 precisa de um IGMP querier (muitas vezes no switch IE ou de distribuição) para manter as adesões.

pt.question: Como é que o PROFINET RT transporta os dados cíclicos em tempo real?
options: Dentro de sessões ISO-TSAP na porta TCP 102
Diretamente em tramas Ethernet com Ethertype 0x8892
Em pacotes UDP 2222 em multicast para todas as células
Em tópicos MQTT publicados num broker central
pt.explanation: O PROFINET RT salta a pilha IP/UDP nos dados cíclicos e usa tramas Layer 2 com Ethertype 0x8892, normalmente com prioridade 802.1Q. Por isso não pode ser encaminhado por routers.

pt.question: Que ficheiro descreve à ferramenta de engenharia os módulos e parâmetros de um equipamento PROFINET?
options: Ficheiro GSDML
Ficheiro MIB
Ficheiro EDS
Módulo YANG
pt.explanation: Os equipamentos PROFINET trazem um ficheiro GSDML (descrição geral da estação em XML). Os ficheiros EDS têm o mesmo papel em EtherNet/IP e DeviceNet.

pt.question: Um IO-Device PROFINET substituído não começa a trocar dados. Por que é que o IO-Controller o identifica?
options: Pelo número de série impresso na etiqueta de características
Pelo tempo de concessão e hostname DHCP
Apenas pelo endereço MAC gravado de fábrica
Pelo nome de dispositivo PROFINET, definido por DCP
pt.explanation: O PROFINET identifica os equipamentos pelo nome. O controlador encontra o nome através do DCP e só depois atribui o IP; um equipamento novo sem o nome certo (ou sem nomeação por topologia) fica calado.

pt.question: Que variante de PROFINET é necessária para controlo de movimento bem sincronizado com jitter abaixo de 1 µs?
options: PROFINET IRT (Conformance Class C)
PROFINET RT sobre Wi-Fi
PROFINET sobre Modbus TCP
PROFINET NRT sobre UDP
pt.explanation: O IRT (tempo real isócrono, Conformance Class C) reserva janelas de tempo em switches com suporte em hardware e consegue jitter abaixo do microssegundo. O RT (classes A/B) chega para a maior parte do I/O.

pt.question: O que é o PROFIsafe?
options: Uma camada de segurança funcional sobre 'canal negro'
Uma firewall feita só para tráfego PROFINET em células
Um túnel VPN cifrado entre dois PLC remotos
Um cabo PROFINET verde com blindagem dupla extra
pt.explanation: O PROFIsafe acrescenta mecanismos de segurança funcional (contadores, watchdog, CRC, identificadores) sobre PROFINET ou PROFIBUS, tratando a rede como canal negro não fiável. É segurança funcional, não cibersegurança.

pt.question: Que protocolo de redundância em anel está normalizado na IEC 62439-2 e é muito usado com PROFINET?
options: DLR
REP
HSRP
MRP
pt.explanation: O MRP (Media Redundancy Protocol, IEC 62439-2) tem um gestor de anel que bloqueia uma porta até o anel partir. O DLR é o anel EtherNet/IP da ODVA e o REP é da Cisco.

pt.question: O que faz o Cisco REP (Resilient Ethernet Protocol) num anel de switches IE?
options: Duplica cada trama em duas LAN separadas
Bloqueia uma porta por segmento e desbloqueia-a na falha
Substitui todas as VLAN por um único segmento encaminhado
Cifra as tramas entre vizinhos do anel
pt.explanation: O REP organiza um segmento de switches, mantém uma porta alternativa bloqueada para evitar o loop e desbloqueia-a depressa quando um link falha. É mais rápido do que o STP clássico em anéis.

pt.question: Porque é que o PRP (IEC 62439-3) tem tempo de recuperação zero depois de uma falha de link?
options: O controlador retransmite mais depressa do que o RPI
Os switches pré-calculam um caminho de reserva com OSPF LFA
O gestor do anel desbloqueia a porta em 1 ms
Cada trama vai por duas LAN independentes e o recetor descarta o duplicado
pt.explanation: Um nó PRP com dupla ligação envia cada trama pela LAN A e pela LAN B ao mesmo tempo; o recetor fica com a primeira cópia e descarta a segunda, por isso uma falha única não perde nada.

pt.question: Em que é que o HSR difere do PRP?
options: O HSR envia as duas cópias à volta de um único anel
O HSR precisa de duas redes paralelas totalmente separadas
O HSR só funciona em ligações sem fios
O HSR é um protocolo de routing para WAN OT
pt.explanation: O HSR (High-availability Seamless Redundancy) envia as duas cópias em sentidos opostos à volta de um anel de nós com suporte HSR. O PRP usa duas LAN paralelas independentes.

pt.question: Um PLC com uma só ligação tem de entrar numa rede PRP. Que equipamento o liga às duas LAN?
options: Um conversor de media de cobre para fibra
Uma RedBox (caixa de redundância)
Uma workgroup bridge Wi-Fi
Um injetor PoE de 802.3at na linha
pt.explanation: Uma RedBox liga nós com uma só ligação (SAN) a PRP ou HSR, enviando e recebendo as tramas duplicadas em nome deles.

pt.question: Que protocolo em anel foi definido pela ODVA para equipamentos EtherNet/IP com switch embutido de duas portas?
options: MRP
PRP
DLR
REP
pt.explanation: O DLR (Device Level Ring) permite a equipamentos EtherNet/IP com duas portas formar um anel; um supervisor de anel envia beacons e desbloqueia a sua porta quando o anel parte.

pt.question: Que característica é típica de um switch Ethernet industrial (IE) em comparação com um de escritório?
options: Montagem em calha DIN e gama de temperatura alargada
Um controlador wireless incorporado
Só portas de 10 Mb/s por compatibilidade
Arrefecimento obrigatório com ventoinha interna
pt.explanation: Os switches IE são robustos: montagem em calha DIN ou painel, sem ventoinha, temperatura alargada, resistência a vibração, duas entradas de alimentação e relés de alarme.

pt.question: Para que serve o contacto de relé de alarme em muitos switches IE?
options: Fazer reset ao switch remotamente com uma escrita Modbus
Alimentar diretamente sensores de campo a 24 V DC
Sinalizar falhas, como perda de alimentação, a um PLC
Sincronizar os relógios da célula com o grandmaster PTP
pt.explanation: O relé de alarme de contacto seco muda de estado em falhas configuradas (perda de uma fonte, porta em baixo, temperatura) para que uma entrada de PLC ou um sinalizador possa reagir.

pt.question: Um fabricante de máquinas entrega dez células idênticas, todas com 192.168.1.0/24. Como podem entrar numa só rede de fábrica sem mudar endereços?
options: Pôr as dez células na mesma VLAN e deixar o ARP resolver
Usar NAT de Layer 2 (1:1) nas células
Usar PROFIsafe nos uplinks das células para a fábrica
Desligar o ARP nos controladores de cada linha
pt.explanation: O NAT de Layer 2 nos switches IE traduz 1:1 os endereços privados de cada célula para endereços únicos da fábrica, permitindo instalar várias vezes a mesma imagem de máquina.

pt.question: Porque é que uma linha de produção longa pode usar topologia em anel em vez de estrela redundante?
options: Os anéis dão sempre menos latência ponta a ponta do que as estrelas
Um anel precisa de muito menos cabo ao longo da linha
Os anéis dispensam qualquer protocolo de redundância ou de loop
As estrelas não transportam protocolos industriais
pt.explanation: Ao longo de uma linha comprida, encadear os switches num anel gasta muito menos cabo do que levar dois uplinks de cada switch até à distribuição, e continua a aguentar a falha de um link.

pt.question: Que protocolo usa uma subestação ou sistema de movimento quando precisa de precisão de relógio abaixo do microssegundo?
options: Carimbos de tempo do syslog
NTP pela Internet
SNTP a partir de um PC
IEEE 1588 PTP
pt.explanation: O IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol chega a precisão abaixo do microssegundo com carimbo de tempo em hardware; o NTP fica normalmente na ordem dos milissegundos.

pt.question: No PTP, como é escolhido o relógio grandmaster?
options: Pelo endereço IP mais baixo configurado na VLAN
Pelo Best Master Clock Algorithm (BMCA)
Pelo switch com mais portas ativas no anel
Pelo stratum NTP anunciado pelo PLC
pt.explanation: Os relógios trocam mensagens Announce e o BMCA compara priority1, classe do relógio, exatidão, variância, priority2 e identidade para eleger o melhor grandmaster.

pt.question: O que faz um switch que é transparent clock no PTP?
options: Passa a grandmaster quando o GPS falha
Termina o PTP e começa um domínio novo
Junta o seu tempo de residência num campo de correção
Bloqueia as mensagens Sync que chegam às portas de acesso
pt.explanation: Um transparent clock mede quanto tempo cada mensagem de evento PTP ficou dentro do switch e escreve-o no correctionField, para que o atraso de fila não estrague a precisão. Um boundary clock, pelo contrário, termina e regenera o PTP.

pt.question: Que perfil PTP é usado em subestações IEC 61850?
options: O perfil telecom da ITU-T
O Power Profile (IEEE C37.238 / IEC 61850-9-3)
O perfil de áudio/vídeo bridging IEEE 802.1AS
O perfil default com recurso a NTP
pt.explanation: As subestações usam o Power Profile (IEEE C37.238, IEC/IEEE 61850-9-3), com transporte Layer 2 e atraso peer-to-peer. As fábricas usam normalmente o perfil default (CIP Sync).

pt.question: Na IEC 62443, o que é uma conduta (conduit)?
options: Uma calha para cabos OT blindados
Um caminho de comunicação controlado entre zonas
Uma cópia de segurança dos programas do PLC
Uma alimentação redundante de um armário de controlo
pt.explanation: A IEC 62443 junta em zonas os ativos com necessidades de segurança parecidas; as condutas são os canais de comunicação entre zonas, onde se aplicam controlos como firewalls.

pt.question: O que descrevem os níveis de segurança (SL 1 a 4) da IEC 62443?
options: Quantas firewalls a fábrica tem de comprar para cada zona
O número máximo de contas de utilizador permitidas por zona
O nível de integridade de segurança (SIL) exigido a uma máquina
Proteção contra atacantes mais capazes
pt.explanation: O SL 1 protege contra violações casuais ou acidentais e o SL 4 contra atacantes sofisticados com muitos recursos. Os SL são definidos como alvo por zona e conduta.

pt.question: Que parte da IEC 62443 lista os requisitos técnicos de segurança de um sistema de controlo no seu conjunto?
pt.explanation: A 62443-3-3 define os requisitos de segurança do sistema e os níveis de segurança. A 4-1 trata do ciclo de desenvolvimento seguro do fabricante, a 4-2 dos requisitos por componente e a 2-1 do programa de segurança do dono do ativo.

pt.question: Porque é que a monitorização passiva é preferida à análise ativa para o inventário de ativos OT?
options: As ferramentas passivas encontram mais portas TCP
As análises ativas são proibidas por lei em todas as fábricas
A monitorização passiva não precisa de qualquer acesso à rede
Alguns PLC podem bloquear ou falhar quando analisados
pt.explanation: Controladores frágeis ou antigos podem bloquear com análises agressivas. Ferramentas passivas como o Cisco Cyber Vision aprendem os ativos a partir de tráfego espelhado e inspeção profunda dos protocolos industriais.

pt.question: O que normaliza principalmente a ISA-95?
options: Os algoritmos de cifra exigidos nas atualizações de firmware dos PLC
As cores de cabo e pinagens dos conectores Ethernet da fábrica
A integração entre sistemas empresariais e o controlo da produção
Os canais de rádio permitidos para sensores sem fios na fábrica
pt.explanation: A ISA-95 (IEC 62264) define funções, níveis e modelos de dados para integrar os sistemas do negócio (nível 4, ERP) com as operações de produção (nível 3, MOM/MES).

pt.question: No modelo Purdue, que nível contém os próprios sensores, válvulas e motores?
options: Nível 0
Nível 2
Nível 3
Nível 1
pt.explanation: O nível 0 é o processo físico: sensores, atuadores, válvulas, motores. Os controladores que os leem e comandam estão no nível 1.

pt.question: Onde colocaria normalmente o historian da fábrica, o controlador de domínio OT e os servidores de patches da linha?
options: Nível 3, operações do site na zona industrial
Nível 4, no datacenter da empresa junto ao ERP
Nível 1, junto aos PLC de cada célula
Nível 0, na rede de instrumentos do processo
pt.explanation: O nível 3 (operações do site) aloja serviços de toda a fábrica, como o historian, o AD de OT, servidores de patches e antivírus e estações de engenharia, ainda dentro da zona industrial.

pt.question: Porque é que os desenhos CPwE da Cisco/Rockwell mantêm cada zona de célula/área pequena, com a sua própria VLAN?
options: Para conter broadcasts, falhas e tráfego em tempo real localmente
Para não precisar de firewall nenhuma na IDMZ
Para dar a cada célula a sua própria root bridge de spanning tree diferente
Para permitir encaminhar PROFINET RT entre áreas
pt.explanation: Zonas de célula/área pequenas limitam os domínios de broadcast e multicast, mantêm local o I/O crítico e impedem que uma falha ou tempestade numa célula se espalhe a toda a fábrica.

pt.question: O que torna o OPC UA atrativo para troca de dados entre IT e OT?
options: Só funcionar entre equipamentos do mesmo fabricante e da mesma gama
Tramas Layer 2 que dispensam qualquer endereço IP
Substituir a cablagem de fieldbus por loops 4–20 mA
Segurança incorporada e um modelo de informação rico
pt.explanation: O OPC UA é independente do fabricante, usa um modelo de informação estruturado e inclui autenticação, assinatura e cifra. O protocolo binário usa por omissão TCP 4840.

pt.question: Como é que o MQTT entrega os dados de sensores de muitos equipamentos edge?
options: Os publicadores enviam para tópicos num broker; os subscritores recebem
Cada cliente interroga todos os sensores, um a um, num ciclo round-robin fixo
Os equipamentos enviam tramas em multicast com Ethertype 0x88B8
Os sensores escrevem diretamente nas tabelas da base de dados do ERP central
pt.explanation: O MQTT é publish/subscribe sobre TCP (1883, ou 8883 com TLS): os equipamentos publicam em tópicos num broker e qualquer cliente subscrito recebe as mensagens.

pt.question: O que garante o QoS 2 do MQTT?
options: A mensagem é entregue no máximo uma vez, sem nova tentativa
A mensagem é entregue exatamente uma vez ao recetor
O broker comprime a carga útil antes de a reencaminhar
A mensagem é cifrada ponta a ponta sem precisar de TLS
pt.explanation: O QoS 0 é no máximo uma vez, o QoS 1 pelo menos uma vez (pode haver duplicados) e o QoS 2 exatamente uma vez, com um handshake de quatro passos. O QoS não tem nada a ver com cifra.

pt.question: Que protocolo é típico entre um SCADA master de uma utility e as estações remotas, usando TCP/UDP 20000?
options: BACnet/IP
PROFINET IRT
Modbus RTU
DNP3
pt.explanation: O DNP3 é muito usado em utilities elétricas e de águas para telemetria master–estação remota, com armazenamento de eventos e carimbos de tempo; sobre IP usa a porta 20000.

pt.question: Numa subestação IEC 61850, como são transportadas as mensagens GOOSE de disparo?
options: Tópicos MQTT com QoS 2 para a sala de controlo
Sessões TCP ao servidor MMS na porta 102
Tramas Layer 2 multicast com prioridade alta
Traps SNMP enviadas para o gestor de rede
pt.explanation: As mensagens GOOSE são publicadas diretamente como multicast Layer 2 (Ethertype 0x88B8) com prioridade de VLAN e repetidas depressa, para cumprir tempos de proteção de poucos milissegundos.

pt.question: Que protocolo se encontra sobretudo em automação de edifícios (AVAC, iluminação) e usa UDP 47808?
options: BACnet/IP
EtherCAT
CC-Link IE
pt.explanation: O BACnet/IP é o protocolo comum de automação de edifícios e usa UDP 47808 (0xBAC0). O IEC 104 é para telecomando da rede elétrica sobre TCP 2404.

pt.question: Porque é que as firewalls normais de escritório, sozinhas, protegem mal os protocolos industriais?
options: Não conseguem filtrar tráfego nenhum que use a porta TCP 502
Só funcionam com equipamentos industriais em IPv6
Muitas vezes não inspecionam comandos como escritas no PLC
Bloqueiam automaticamente todo o tráfego multicast
pt.explanation: Uma regra por porta não distingue uma leitura Modbus de uma escrita nem um comando CIP 'parar PLC'. Firewalls e IDS com conhecimento industrial usam DPI para permitir ou alertar por função.

pt.question: Que parte da IEC 62443 se dirige às práticas de desenvolvimento seguro dos fabricantes de produtos?
pt.explanation: A 62443-4-1 define o ciclo de desenvolvimento seguro de produtos para fornecedores. A 3-2 trata da avaliação de risco e desenho de zonas/condutas e a 2-4 dos requisitos para prestadores de serviços.

pt.question: Numa avaliação IEC 62443-3-2, qual é o resultado para cada zona e conduta?
options: Uma lista obrigatória de marcas
Um nível de segurança alvo (SL-T)
Um prémio de seguro para a fábrica
Um valor fixo de MTBF para os switches
pt.explanation: A 62443-3-2 divide o sistema em zonas e condutas e, com base na avaliação de risco, atribui a cada uma um nível de segurança alvo (SL-T) que depois orienta os controlos exigidos.

pt.question: Qual destes é um dos sete requisitos fundamentais (FR) da IEC 62443?
options: Comprimento máximo de cabo
Fluxo de dados restrito
Dependência do fabricante
Taxas anuais de auditoria
pt.explanation: Os FR são controlo de identificação e autenticação, controlo de uso, integridade do sistema, confidencialidade dos dados, fluxo de dados restrito, resposta atempada a eventos e disponibilidade de recursos.

pt.question: Um fornecedor precisa de acesso remoto a um PLC para suporte. Que abordagem segue as boas práticas de OT?
options: Um reencaminhamento permanente de porta no router de internet
Um modem 4G instalado dentro do armário de controlo da máquina
Partilhar a password do portátil de engenharia com o fornecedor
Um jump host na IDMZ com MFA, aprovação e registo da sessão
